Title: Attackers Exploit AhsayCBS Flaws to Deploy Sandbox-Evading Python Backdoor
Context: The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach...
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an attack that exploited two now-patched vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS to deliver a Python-based implant.

The activity, observed by Huntress in early October 2026, involves the exploitation of a chain comprising CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on affected systems. Patches for the two vulnerabilities were released by Ahsay Backup in mid-October 2026.

The two vulnerabilities are assessed to have been weaponized as zero-days, with the managed security platform first observing threat actors employing a smash-and-grab approach to deploy web shells and XMRig cryptocurrency miners on compromised systems.

"However, this incident reflects a much larger intrusion with more patience; the operator planted shells in several places, ran two different miners, staged tunneling tools, and installed a custom implant, all on servers whose job is to hold backups," Huntress researcher Jonathan Semon said.

Specifically, the unknown threat actor is said to have left five families of Jakarta Server Pages (JSP, formerly JavaServer Pages) web shells -

nsmind.jsp, a signed API with command execution and file transfer capabilities using exec, cd, upload, and download parameters

AhsayCBS.jsp, a loader that hides encrypted payloads in the pixel data of PNG images and runs them from memory

Keyed command shell, which compares a hard-coded key against its own copy and, if it matches, runs the command via "cmd.exe"

Keyed shell with file write, which expands on the keyed command web shell with the ability to write Base64-decoded bytes to any path the service account can reach and deploy more tools

status_<six_random_letters>.jsp or st_<six_random_letters>.jsp (e.g., st_jgaejj.jsp), which are used to run commands, recursively delete any path provided as input, and delete themselves using cmd, del, and rm parameters.

"[AhsayCBS.jsp's] disguise as an internal image preview service even extended down to a comment block describing a watermark endpoint," Huntress explained. "The web shell used only JSP implicit objects and fully qualified class names, meaning it would compile on any servlet container and on Java Development Kit (JDK) 6 and later."

The attack, besides deploying an XMRig miner masquerading as Microsoft Edge, has been found to deliver a second XMRig miner ("kvm-agent.exe") that restarts every minute through a SYSTEM scheduled task, while using a different wallet and mining pool.

The most notable aspect of the intrusion revolves around the Python backdoor ("main.py"), which is designed to run only on the host it's staged on and prevent it from executing within a sandbox or an analyst's machine.

It achieves this by computing the SHA-256 cryptographic hash of the host's MachineGuid and looks for a marker file with the same name in the same directory housing the Python implant, and then runs an embedded x64 DLL in memory that contacts a command-and-control (C2) server ("creepexplosiondarknight[.]com").

In an attempt to fly under the radar, the attack chain also configures Microsoft Defender exclusions, while serving tunneling tools (GOST and Chisel) and legitimate remote access software (AnyDesk, Atera, and Splashtop) to establish persistent access.

Evidence indicates that the threat actor may have targeted servers holding or managing backups.

"On a related Veeam server in the same environment, we also saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module: a PowerShell script, apparently launched remotely through WMI, that queried the VeeamBackup PostgreSQL database for stored credentials and decrypted them with DPAPI," Semon said.

"Backup software holds credentials for hypervisors, repositories and domain accounts. We cannot say how many of those credentials were retrieved, but the pairing of an Ahsay foothold with a Veeam credential query suggested the operator was interested in backup infrastructure on purpose, not by accident."

Title: Binance Warns of iOS Sandbox Escape That Could Expose Crypto Wallet Keys, No Fix Confirmed
Context: Apple's updates for iOS 26 and 27, released yesterday, do not list a fix
Full Text:
An iOS sandbox escape published on GitHub lets an app read other apps' files on iPhones running iOS 26 and 27. That puts seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials at risk of exposure to malicious apps, Binance warned today. Apple's updates for iOS 26 and 27, released yesterday, do not list a fix.

A researcher who goes by forcequit released the escape, called worse_query, on Sunday, a day before those updates came out. Neither the exchange nor the researcher reported any attacks or thefts involving it.

The exchange told users to delete apps installed from untrusted sources, such as sideloaded or manually signed apps, and to update iOS and all their apps. No fix for the escape has been confirmed.

For anyone who suspects a breach, the exchange's security warning advises moving funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and resetting all active login sessions.

The researcher's proof-of-concept code can reach every app's data container on an iPhone, and some system folders on iOS 27. To use it, an app has to set up an App Group container.

He says the code is for developers and "isn't useful by itself." Other developers have built apps on it that people can install.

One of them is WQ Files, a file manager that developer Christoph Kolbicz built on worse_query. It reaches other apps' data without a jailbreak or a kernel exploit, and it can edit, delete and clear that data.

WQ Files installs via sideloading tools such as AltStore and SideStore, which automatically create the App Group it needs when used with an Apple ID. No one involved has said whether an app from the App Store could use worse_query.

The three versions in the exchange's warning are the ones listed as tested in the WQ Files release notes. The researcher gives a wider range.

Of these sources, only Erosion's developers list iOS 27.2.1, which came out yesterday, and none lists iOS 26.7.3. They added 27.2.1 this week in a README change with the note "pretty sure 27.2.1 is supported".

Yesterday's updates, iOS 27.2.1 and iOS 26.7.3, fixed two iMessage flaws and several Bluetooth bugs. The security notes for iOS 27.2.1 do not mention worse_query or any sandbox issues, nor do the iOS 26.7.3 notes. Apple does not disclose, discuss, or confirm security issues until it has investigated and a patch or release is available, the notes say.

In a reply on X, the researcher wrote that he had not planned to release worse_query early. He added that "Apple was stalling on responding to me and people started larping with it on here."

The exchange did not name any wallet app as exposed, and neither did the researcher nor the developers of the apps built on worse_query.

Vulnerability Details

This vulnerability allows local attackers to execute arbitrary code on affected installations of Docker Sandboxes. User interaction is required to exploit this vulnerability in that the target must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file.

The specific flaw exists within the creation of sandboxes using the clone mode. The issue results from launching an executable from an untrusted location. An attacker can leverage this vulnerability to execute code in the context of the current user.

Docker has issued an update to correct this vulnerability. More details can be found at: https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-121614

Title: Beyond the Endpoint: Rethinking Security for the Modern Workspace
Context: Endpoint security, identity protection, email security, vulnerability management, data protection, and detection and response have each become important parts of the security stack
Full Text:
The way we work has changed significantly, and now the way we secure that work is changing with it. Again.

For years, organizations have added security technologies to address new risk categories as they emerged. Endpoint security, identity protection, email security, vulnerability management, data protection, and detection and response have each become important parts of the security stack.

But today's attacks rarely stay within one of those boundaries. This shift is driving a broader approach to protecting the modern digital worker: Workspace Security.

How Do You Define Workspace Security?

The workspace has become an interconnected attack surface, and workspace security looks beyond traditional boundaries to focus on the ways attackers now reach users and business data. Several shifts are accelerating this pivot toward workplace security.

1. Work is increasingly distributed. Endpoints, mobile devices, browsers, SaaS applications, and cloud services have extended work far beyond the corporate network.

2. Identity has become a critical security boundary. Attackers don't always need to break through traditional defenses if they can log in using compromised credentials, tokens, or sessions.

3. Applications and collaboration tools are part of the attack surface. Email, browsers, SaaS, and collaboration platforms connect users directly to business data and provide attackers with more opportunities to target them.

4. AI is adding another interaction layer. Generative AI and copilots are quickly becoming part of everyday workflows, creating new interactions between users, applications, and organizational data. It is also increasing the need for visibility and control into how AI is being used and what data it can access.

Rather than isolated changes, these shifts increasingly overlap within the same workflows and the same attacks.

What are the Risks of Operating Security in Silos?

Because users, identities, devices, applications, data, and AI are interconnected, protecting each in isolation leaves gaps between them.

Security architectures have traditionally been organized around individual control points. Endpoint tools protect devices. Identity tools protect accounts and access. Email security protects communications. Other technologies manage vulnerabilities, applications, and data.

Attackers see the environment differently.

A phishing email might lead to credential theft. Those credentials could provide access to a legitimate application. From there, an attacker may establish persistence, elevate privileges, move across systems, or access sensitive information.

One attack can therefore generate signals across the environment.

How Are Organizations Breaking Down Cybersecurity Silos?

According to Gartner®, "Cybersecurity teams with limited resources and a need to reduce silos require a simpler, more unified approach to securing digital work than traditional multivendor tool stacks. WCPs address this by preintegrating modules to lower costs, reduce errors, and improve cybersecurity posture."

Is Endpoint Security a Key Part of Workspace Security?

The endpoint remains central to the evolution toward workspace security, especially because unified endpoint security platforms have expanded beyond malware protection to include numerous capabilities: attack surface reduction, behavioral detection, and vulnerability and patch management, along with EDR, XDR, and identity threat protection.

At the same time, the risks surrounding the digital worker increasingly extend beyond the endpoint itself. Gartner notes, "WCPs have replaced Gartner’s coverage of the extended detection and response (XDR) market, which no longer exists in its original form. As vendors expanded native modules and improved integration, XDR became a feature within WCPs and other cybersecurity markets."

Workspace Security isn't about making endpoint protection less important. It is about extending its context and connecting protection around the digital worker. This is why the distinction between a collection of security products and an integrated platform is significant.

Integration makes the security controls surrounding the user work together more effectively.

What Does Effective Workspace Security Look Like?

Workspace Security is an evolving approach that brings the protections surrounding digital workers together more cohesively, connecting proactive risk reduction, prevention, detection, and response across the workspace. Organizations evaluating their approach should consider several key principles:

Broad visibility: Can security teams understand risk and activity across endpoints, identities, applications, data, and emerging technologies such as AI?

Proactive risk reduction and prevention: Can the platform identify vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, identity risks, and other exposures, reduce the attack surface, and prevent threats before they become incidents?

Connected context: Can telemetry across devices, identities, applications, and data be correlated to help teams understand the broader attack rather than investigate individual signals in isolation?

Deep integration: Do capabilities genuinely share telemetry, policies, behavioral analysis, and workflows, or are they simply a collection of products from the same vendor?

Simplified operations: Can teams manage policies, prioritize alerts, investigate threats, and take action through centralized workflows with less context switching?

Openness and flexibility: Can the platform integrate with the wider security ecosystem when specialized capabilities or existing investments are still required?

The goal is to reduce exposure, prevent more threats before they occur, and provide the context needed to detect and respond effectively to attacks.

Securing How Work Happens

Workspace Security represents an important evolution in cybersecurity, but not because organizations suddenly need another security product category.

It reflects a more fundamental change: the way people work is increasingly interconnected, attacks cross traditional security boundaries, and the security protecting digital workers needs to become more connected as well.

For resource-constrained IT and security teams, in particular, the opportunity is significant: fewer silos, better context, stronger prevention, and simpler security operations.

Title: Google dismantles botnet secretly running on 1.3 million Android TV boxes
Context: Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware
Full Text:
Smashing the botnet

Google worked with several other organizations to disrupt the x.cpe network, including Japan’s National Police Agency, Synthient, and Trend Micro. Google says it has taken legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to operate and install its malware. It also went after command-and-control servers operated by Videostrong that were connected to other malware campaigns. Google estimates Videostrong has been cut off from about 10 million compromised devices.

This action should make the affected devices safe to use, but probably not as safe as they should be. Play Protect is still disabled, and the inert malware modules are still installed. Since they are loaded as system apps, users cannot easily remove them.

Synthient has published a list of 182 device model names known to be included in the botnet. Anyone who has purchased a MECOOL or white label Android TV box of unknown origin should check it. Trend Micro counted a total of 1,472,554 infected devices, somewhat higher than Google’s estimate. The overwhelming majority were in Brazil, Malaysia, Iraq, Mexico, and Taiwan, but tens of thousands were also online in the US, Germany, the UK, Australia, and Canada.

Google determined the operation was not the work of a rogue actor, so it has ended its relationship with Videostrong. The company, as well as any subsidiaries, will not be permitted to use Google’s Android apps and services.

Google also notes that it is updating its certification process to close the loophole that allowed Videostrong to operate its botnet on certified devices. Android is open source, though, and there are countless uncertified Android-based TV boxes out there. Videostrong could continue to sell malicious hardware under other brands without Google apps. But it would still have to rebuild its malware operation from scratch.

Title: 3AM Hits European Schools: A Hybrid AI Ransomware Attack, Part Human, Part Agentic Loop
Context: In an AI-generated attack, a model writes the malware itself, often in bulk; our APT36 research described this as “vibeware” (Bitdefender research, March 2026)
Full Text:
I’d like to thank my colleagues, Adrian Schipor and Martin Zugec, for their invaluable contributions to this research.

TL;DR: It is the first case of this kind we have investigated, a hybrid operation in which some parts show a human operator at the keyboard while others behave like an agentic loop, a language model reading each result and retrying with different commands. In this case, a 3AM (ThreeAM) ransomware affiliate breached a European school estate in the UK, then used ordinary Windows tools to build domain trusts and reach other schools.

Three Kinds of AI Attack, and Why This One Is a Hybrid

Attacks that involve AI fall, broadly, into three categories.

In an AI-generated attack, a model writes the malware itself, often in bulk; our APT36 research described this as “vibeware” (Bitdefender research, March 2026).

In an AI-assisted attack, human engineers build the tools and use AI to speed up the work, as we assessed in the SilkParasite campaign (Bitdefender research, August 2026).

In an AI-operated attack, AI works the intrusion itself: it chooses and writes the commands, reads the results and adjusts, the way an attacker at a keyboard would. The first two describe how malware is made. The third describes who, or what, is running the attack.

We prefer putting attacks into buckets like these, but in cybersecurity things often sit in gray areas. In fact, this case we recently investigated does not fit a single bucket. A 3AM ransomware affiliate breached a school in the UK in what we consider a hybrid operation: some parts show a human operator at the keyboard, while others behave like an AI agent working throughout the intrusion.

With the exception of the encryptor itself, the whole operation was built on legitimate, built-in tools, which is standard for ransomware operations. This is living off the land (LOTL): abusing tools already present on the victim’s machines instead of bringing in custom malware. The attacker worked through PowerShell, WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation, the built-in interface for running commands on other machines), reg, netsh, rundll32 and the domain and scheduling utilities that ship with Windows. In our earlier analysis of about 700,000 security incidents, 84% of high-severity attacks involved LOTL binaries (Bitdefender research, June 2025), and four of the five most abused binaries in that study (netsh, PowerShell, reg and rundll32) appear in this intrusion. A handful of public tools were brought in as well, among them an Impacket-style remote execution tool, Mimikatz and a published Veeam script, but nothing in the toolkit is novel. That is the lesson of this case: an AI-enabled attack does not have to be novel or creative to work (The Hacker News, September 2026). It uses the techniques defenders already know.

What is different is how the attacker behaved, and several things point to an agentic loop, a program that feeds each result back to a model and runs what comes back. The commands carry the usual tells of a model: a call to the backup software’s web interface (Veeam, a widely used enterprise backup product) on a port and with a login method that do not match the vendor’s documentation, a mistake typical of writing from memory rather than from the manual (Veeam REST API authorization), along with confirmation files, self-labeled output and numbered revisions of the same script. The retries behave like a loop too.

On 13 September the attacker ran a PowerShell command, re-ran it unchanged 41 seconds later, changed a single call 49 seconds after that, and then, 47 seconds later, abandoned PowerShell for wmic, the older built-in command-line interface to WMI. The complete rewrite arrived as fast as the minor changes before it, and a person writing it by hand would be expected to take noticeably longer. The same held across nine retries:

The delay before the next attempt ran from 40 to 101 seconds whatever the size of the change, while moving on to a new task took minutes.

That split, longer time between tasks and shorter between retries, is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries.

On 13 September, for example, the commands before the retry sequence were simpler and sat two to sixteen minutes apart, the pace of someone reading output and deciding what to do next.

The clearest example of this work is how the attacker joined the estate’s separate Active Directory domains (independent directories of accounts and computers). A domain trust, a configured relationship that lets accounts from one domain log on in another, is mechanical, order-sensitive work: it has to be set up correctly on both sides, names have to resolve between the domains, and one wrong detail stops everything. Here the attacker built the trusts and then ran a series of diagnostic probes and restarted the service that maintains the secure channel between domains.

Our reading, which is interpretation and not a finding, is that this is the kind of work a model suits: repetitive configuration where the fix comes from reading an error and trying again. It is also work a defender can see, because a new trust between domains is a rare change and cheap to alert on.

We were not able to access the machine the attacker worked from, so we cannot document anything about the language model itself: which model it was, whether it ran locally or remotely, or even whether a person was copying and pasting instructions and results between the implant and the model. What we can document is behavior, and the behavior is that of an agentic loop. We present the hybrid reading as the working model defenders should plan around, not as an established fact.

As a European cybersecurity company, we wanted to share the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe. But right now it is one case, an anecdote, and not a trend. In general, most of what Bitdefender MDR sees in real-world investigations is still boring. Vibeware, the clearest example of AI-generated malware, accounts for only about 0.07% of the malware samples we collect each month, and most intrusions we investigate still look the way they did before language models. The attack was not fast: even its quickest retries took 40 seconds or more. “Machine speed” is a phrase that marketing repeats, usually about very expensive incidents backed by frontier-scale infrastructure, and we expect real-world attacks, especially those running local models, to look closer to what we observed. It was not innovative in any way: built-in tools, a few public ones and a commodity encryptor.

What this attack does show is that the hybrid approach works, and we assess that it makes economic sense for attackers, with a person setting the goals and a model handling the mechanical work. We can expect hybrid attacks like this one to become more common in 2027.

Join us for the LIVE discussion: A Hybrid AI Ransomware Attack.

What We Can and Cannot Show

Reports of “AI ransomware” tend to blur three separate claims, and this case supports them to very different degrees.

Claim

Status in this case

A language model generated the commands

Strongly supported by the content of the commands

An agentic loop (a program that feeds each command’s output back to a model and runs whatever it returns) chose each next action

Behaves like one. Retries arrive at a steady pace whatever the size of the change. A person copying and pasting between a shell and a chat window cannot be excluded

No human was involved in the hands-on phase

Unsupported. Nothing in our telemetry bears on it

The second claim rests on the retry cadence described above: a steady delay per attempt, whatever the size of the change, is how a loop that waits on a model behaves. A person pasting output between a shell and a chat window could produce the same rhythm, so we describe the behavior and leave the mechanism open. Our log holds only detected events, so some attempts may be missing and every gap is an upper bound.

The pacing also bears on the third claim, though it cannot settle it. Between tasks, the gaps on 13 September were 5, 2, 14, 16 and 3 minutes, the pace of a person reading each result and choosing what to do next. Between retries, they were under two minutes. That is what a hybrid operation would look like, with a person deciding and a model doing the repetitive work, but a model that simply takes longer to plan a new task could look similar. Nothing in the telemetry rules either reading out.

Telemetry alone cannot close the gap between the three claims, because the machine most likely to hold any automation was an unmanaged host (an internal machine running no Bitdefender agent) that sat outside our visibility. Every attacker action we saw originated there.

Attribution and Victimology

We attribute the intrusion to a 3AM (ThreeAM) ransomware affiliate, and the attribution is confirmed. ThreeAM operates on a ransomware-as-a-service model, in which the core group develops the encryptor and leases it to affiliates who carry out the intrusions and share the proceeds. The encryptor build and its command-line pattern (the host.exe binary invoked with an ID argument and a speed argument, an anti-debugging check, and deletion of Windows system-state backups) are consistent with earlier public ThreeAM analyses.

The encryptor we analyzed is a Rust-based sample, and public tracking lists ThreeAM as first seen in February 2023. The rest of the tradecraft matches the classic affiliate playbook: Impacket-like tools for remote execution, credential theft from Veeam and from Windows endpoints, rogue domain administrators plus two-way trusts to reach separate domains, and removal of EDR agents before encryption. Background on the group is drawn from external tracking (WatchGuard, “ThreeAM”, October 2026).

It is worth saying plainly what is conventional here, because it is most of the operation. The affiliate model, the access, the encryptor, and the choice of a mid-sized public-sector target are all ordinary and human. The sign of a model lives in how the commands behave, not in the strategy behind them.

The target is a school estate in the UK. The machine list held 47 systems: about 21 servers, 8 of them domain controllers (the servers that hold the directory of accounts and enforce logins); 10 workstations still on Windows 10, which left support in October 2025; one domain controller on the older Windows Server 2012 R2; and the rest on Windows 11. The environment began as several separate Active Directory domains (separate account directories) that were not connected to each other.

The attacker’s reconnaissance was specific to the sector. From a domain controller it enumerated trust relationships between domains and searched SYSVOL (the shared folder where Active Directory stores logon scripts, readable by any domain user) for the names and subnets of other schools. The two backdoor domain-administrator accounts it created, library and svc_bkpmon, carried names chosen to blend into a school’s account list.

The Intrusion by Phase

All times are UTC. Each observed behavior is mapped to a MITRE ATT&CK technique, the industry-standard catalog of attacker actions, on first mention. Command-level analysis of the oddities in these steps is held for the next section; here we record what happened, when, and where the outcome is unknown.

Before September: Initial Access and Earlier Activity

We cannot establish two things.

First, initial access is unknown and we do not see how the attacker gained access. Second, two earlier events may or may not be related to this one: in one event, Restricted Admin mode (a remote-desktop mode that lets an account log on with a stolen hash or ticket instead of a password) was enabled on four machines on 23 January 2026. In another event, someone conducted a hand-typed interactive session on 5 June 2026. We treat these as earlier activity of an unconfirmed relationship, not as part of the September timeline.

Credential Theft From the Backup Servers (10 to 11 September)

The attacker’s first recorded September move targeted the backup infrastructure. A modified copy of a public tool (Veeam-Get-Creds.ps1) read the credentials stored in the backup software’s databases on three backup servers and decrypted them with DPAPI (the Windows Data Protection API, which encrypts secrets so only the owning account on that machine can read them back) (T1555 Credentials from Password Stores). Delivery used Impacket-style remote execution (Impacket is an open-source toolkit for running commands on remote Windows machines; see our explainer) (T1021.002 SMB/Windows Admin Shares). The first command ran through WMI, while the next two ran as services, with services.exe as the parent process, the pattern of service-based modules such as Impacket’s smbexec or psexec. A Chrome Login Data file, which holds saved browser passwords, was copied from a terminal server (T1555.003 Credentials from Web Browsers).

The public tool (Veeam-Get-Creds.ps1) reads the database server, instance and database names from the registry. The strongest signal is a cluster of mistakes typical of generating commands from recalled knowledge rather than from documentation or trial and error.

Title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
Context: A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co
Full Text:
Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user’s Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet’s access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

A report from the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said Google has severed ties with Videostrong Technology Co., a TV box manufacturer in China that GTIG and other industry experts concluded was responsible for including malware that enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes in a botnet dubbed “XCPE” (named after one of the malware’s core code components).

The global distribution of XCPE botnet infections. Image: Google Threat Intelligence Group.

The report said the XCPE botnet loaded the user’s device with software that makes their Internet address available for resale by multiple “residential proxy” services, which allow customers to rent Internet addresses as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

“Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices,” the GTIG post reads, noting that Google took legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install additional malware. “A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors.”

The report notes that while TV boxes made up the the majority of the botnet, the same XCPE malware was found in other Android-based IoT products, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and even digital signage systems.

Google said it requires all Android device makers to pass compatibility and security tests to ensure their products don’t harm users, but that Videostrong nevertheless found a way to load their malicious software immediately after a user boots up one of these devices for the first time (Google says it has since addressed that weakness).

The GTIG report calls out a number of residential proxy providers whose software development kits were routinely downloaded by devices infected by the XCPE botnet. Those include AppSalt, also known as Honeygain, which is owned by the Vilnius, Lithuania-based Oxylabs. In October 2026, Oxylabs was relaunched under a new brand called Source, after receiving $130 million in funding from private equity firm Warburg Pincus that reportedly valued the business at $3.6 billion. Oxylabs did not respond to a request for comment.

Another provider linked to the botnet was NetNut, a once sprawling residential proxy company operated by the publicly-traded Israeli company Alarum Technologies. In July 2026, the FBI worked with industry partners to seize hundreds of domains associated with NetNut, saying the company was responsible for operating a separate botnet called Popa that enslaved TV boxes as residential proxies. Other proxy providers named in the GTIG report include EarnFM, Traffmonetizer, Jaguar, LINKFOG, BMW/IPWeb and GaGaNode.

Google’s announcement credits a number of industry partners, including Synthient, a startup that tracks proxy providers. In January 2026, Synthient published research into the rapid spread of the Kimwolf botnet, which at the time was hammering networks worldwide with record-smashing DDoS attacks. Synthient documented how Kimwolf infected millions of Android set-top boxes virtually overnight, using a widespread vulnerability in these residential proxy services to compromise other Android-based devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting TV box users.

Synthient’s research caused dozens of residential proxy providers to patch their networks, which helped to fragment the Kimwolf botnet into much smaller pieces that made its incessant and disruptive DDoS attacks far easier for network operators to manage. It also attracted the attention of the Motion Picture Association (MPA), a trade group representing the major Hollywood studios, which partnered with Synthient to purchase and tear apart a number of popular Android TV set-top boxes — including some that were being infected by Kimwolf and other IoT botnets.

In a report published today, Synthient examined a popular, pre-infected TV box sold under the brand MECOOL by a publicly traded company in China called Skyworth Technology, concluding that MECOOL also bundled the malware from Videostrong Technology Co. and likewise installed AppSalt/Honeygain and other proxy components.

The MECOOL storefront and marketing. Image: Synthient.com.

Synthient founder Ben Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity that Videostrong’s malware also distributed software for the proxy service Grass. In our November 2025 story, “Is Your Android TV Streaming Box Part of a Botnet?” we quoted a researcher from Censys who found the popular Superbox TV streaming device bundled Grass’s residential proxy software. We also quoted the Grass founder, who denied any affiliation with the TV box maker.

That November 2025 story noted that Superbox and similar Android TV set-top boxes gain new customers primarily by engaging influencers on Tiktok and other social networks who praise the product’s ability to offer hundreds of (pirated) pay TV streaming services for a one-time fee.

Likewise, Synthient’s report observes that the MECOOL set-top boxes exploded in popularity after the product was endorsed in 2023 by the Youtube channel Linux Tech Tips, which has an audience of nearly 17 million subscribers.

The popular Youtube channel Linus Tech Tips discussing MECOOL TV streaming boxes.

The GTIG report estimates the XCPE botnet takedown should sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices, noting that the various proxy and ad fraud affiliates of Videostrong “each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE.”

Synthient’s Brundage echoed that conclusion, calling the 1.3 million number “highly conservative.”

“The scale of affected devices is likely way higher,” he said. “This is probably the largest operation against backdoored TV boxes that we’ve seen.”

Title: Industry Takedown of Botnet Hidden in More Than 1.3 Million TV Set-Top Boxes across 200 Countries
Context: It's proof that collaboration is one of the most powerful tools we have against threats that cross borders and industries
Full Text:
Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Synthient and Japan's National Police Agency form coordinated effort combining security research, threat intelligence and network expertise to identify and disrupt X.CPE botnet

MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif., Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Today, a group of private and public sector partners announced a coordinated takedown of X.CPE, a global botnet hidden in more than 1.3 million set-top boxes across more than 200 countries. Hidden on devices before they were ever sold, the botnet used subscribers' devices and home internet connections without their knowledge or consent. This takedown was led by Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security and Synthient, along with Japan's National Police Agency.

"Operations like this raise the cost for criminals and show that the infrastructure they rely on isn't out of reach," said Charley Snyder, Head of Disruption Operations at Google Threat Intelligence Group. "Disrupting X.CPE took partners across industry working together. It's proof that collaboration is one of the most powerful tools we have against threats that cross borders and industries."

A familiar device hiding an unfamiliar threat

X.CPE was embedded in firmware, the software that controls a device's basic operations, before set-top boxes reached subscribers' homes. X.CPE was built to evade pre-release security checks, and Google has since updated its review process in response, as well as banned the responsible OEM and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Unlike infections that depend on a user opening a suspicious attachment or installing an application, this threat arrived as part of the device itself. Subscribers received no consent request, notification or opt-out options.

Google, Plume, TrendAI™, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Synthient, working with Japan's National Police Agency, carried out a coordinated disruption campaign against X.CPE. Each organization contributed in its own way, applying its expertise in connected-device security, malware analysis, network visibility and digital fraud to analyze the botnet and disrupt its operations.

Together they dismantled a threat hiding behind seemingly routine device activity: software embedded in TV set-top boxes that gave botnet controllers remote access and allowed them to exploit home broadband connections without subscriber consent. The takedown also disrupted the command-and-control domains that operate the criminal affiliates' malware modules. Because these affiliates distribute their modules through channels beyond X.CPE, Google assesses that taking down these domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.

The effort demonstrates the importance of connecting intelligence across organizations to confront threats that cross technology and network boundaries. By bringing together distinct perspectives on compromised devices, malicious software and internet traffic, the partners supported a coordinated takedown aimed at disrupting unauthorized access and monetization and addressing risks to subscriber privacy, broadband resources and trust in connected devices.

Turning home broadband into a business without permission

The botnet generated revenue from compromised devices in a variety of ways, including: reselling bandwidth, delivering video content, ad fraud, loading additional backdoors and, in earlier versions, installing apps for payment.

Title: Sandbox Flipped to ‘Danger-Full-Access’: Unauthorized AI Relays Create Risk for Organizations
Context: Threat Hunter has found the relay in use across a dozen organizations since early 2026
Full Text:
Key findings

An unauthorized relay service has been observed installing the genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code CLIs on enterprise systems and then reconfiguring them to route every request through third-party infrastructure instead of the vendors' own servers.

The service has been active since at least early 2026, and has impacted systems at a dozen organizations, most of them in mainland China, as well as multinational subsidiaries based in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Affected sectors include industrial automation, electronics manufacturing, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, tire manufacturing, petrochemicals, and data center services.

Delivery relies on a fileless PowerShell or bash setup script that is fetched from a lookalike domain by a one-line command that users appear to run themselves shortly after a legitimate install of the Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, so the download looks like a normal companion step rather than an attack. The reconfiguration disables the CLI's execution sandbox entirely, enables network access for the write sandbox, replaces the user's real API credentials with relay-issued tokens, and disables telemetry and error reporting.

On at least one host, the script forced the user to log out of their legitimate Anthropic session and deleted their authentication environment variables before reissuing relay-controlled credentials.

There is no evidence so far that the relay operator has abused this level of access, but a potential risk is that the configuration it installs would let it read every prompt, file, and secret passed through the agent and run commands with the user's full privileges.

The relay's backend infrastructure has rotated across at least eight domains over the observation period, all impersonating OpenAI- or Anthropic-branded chat services.

Overview

AI coding agents such as OpenAI's Codex and Claude Code read files, write code, and run commands on the machines where they are installed. One of the safeguards they employ is a sandbox that is meant to limit what they can do. However, Symantec's Threat Hunter Team has identified an unauthorized relay service that provides access to OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code command-line coding agents, mainly in markets where the vendors do not officially operate, primarily mainland China. Rather than building its own client software, the service repurposes the genuine CLI tools. It installs them normally, then rewrites their configuration to switch sandboxing off, in Codex's case by setting it to “danger-full-access,” and routes every request through its own servers instead of OpenAI's or Anthropic's.

This is not a vulnerability in Codex or Claude Code. The tools are behaving as designed once their configuration has been changed.

Threat Hunter has found the relay in use across a dozen organizations since early 2026. There is no evidence the operator is currently abusing its position, but the configuration changes it makes strip out the safeguards that are meant to contain an AI coding agent, potentially exposing any organization whose employees use it to security risks.

Usage

The organizations where this relay has been observed span industrial automation, electronics manufacturing, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, tire manufacturing, petrochemicals, and data center services. Most are based in mainland China, though the list also includes the Chinese operations, and in some cases the home-market operations, of multinational electronics and petrochemical firms based in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Most instances appear to be a workplace where an employee or the organization itself wanted to use a Western AI coding assistant that is not officially sold in their market and so turned to an unauthorized reseller to get it.

Tooling

Installation and delivery

The service does not distribute a modified or trojanized client. Users run a legitimate npm install

-g @openai/codex, npm install -g codex-cli, or npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code

shortly before the override occurs, within minutes to roughly half an hour.

A fileless PowerShell or bash setup script, fetched with a one-line iwr -useb <url> | iex or curl | bash from a lookalike domain such as vibe.aiok[.]me, checks whether Node.js and the target CLI are already installed, installs them silently if not, and only then applies its own configuration. Because the script performs a real, working installation of the genuine tool, the installation looks routine to the user and to most monitoring tools.

We did not observe any automated or exploit-based delivery. The one-line command embeds a relay-issued API key and the relay's own endpoint, and the script is written for interactive use (it prints progress messages in Chinese and tells the user to re-run it in an elevated PowerShell session if it lacks administrator rights), which indicates that users copy a ready-made command from the relay or its reseller and run it themselves, although we have not seen the page or message it was copied from.

Configuration override

The script's actual purpose is to rewrite each tool's configuration file: ~/.codex/config.toml for Codex, or ~/.claude/settings.json for Claude Code. It replaces the base_url (or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL) with a domain the relay controls, swaps in a relay-issued API key formatted to match what the CLI expects, and establishes both as user-scope environment variables so the change survives a reboot without further action from the operator. It also sets the CLI's sandbox mode to full access and enables network access for the write sandbox, disabling the isolation that is meant to limit what an AI agent can do on the host. Telemetry and error reporting are disabled at the same time, which would also suppress any usage signal that might otherwise reach OpenAI or Anthropic.

sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access" network_access = "true" DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1

Credential replacement

On one host, the script went further before applying its own configuration. It ran claude /logout, deleted the ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variables, and then ran claude /login. That sequence clears out a legitimate, already-authenticated session so it cannot override the credentials the script is about to install. Whether this step runs in every deployment of the script or was specific to that host was not established.

claude /logout Remove-Item Env:ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, Env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue claude /login

Geolocation check

Several hosts show the script querying the Windows locale setting immediately after installation. This is consistent with a service confirming it is running on a system in the region it serves before completing setup.

reg.exe QUERY "HKCU\Control Panel\International\Geo" /v Nation /reg:64

Possible business model

Why an operator would want this degree of control over a client-side relay is unclear. Bypassing the regional restrictions that keep Western AI vendors from selling directly into certain markets is the simplest explanation, but it does not require disabling a CLI's sandbox or establishing persistent credentials that survive a reboot. Reselling capacity below market rates is another possibility: the Claude Code keys issued by the relay were formatted sk-ant-oat01-, the prefix Anthropic uses for subscription-based OAuth tokens rather than sk-ant-api03- pay-per-use API keys, which is consistent with, though not proof of, a relay pooling flat-rate subscriptions and splitting the capacity across many customers. Fraud involving stolen credentials or payment cards, and resale of the prompts and files that pass through the relay, are also plausible and cannot be ruled out with the evidence available.

Significance

To be clear about what we have and haven't observed: the configuration changes described above were observed; the risks that follow from them are potential.

The geography of this activity tracks the practical reality that OpenAI and Anthropic do not officially sell their coding agents into mainland China, which creates demand for unauthorized resellers regardless of who ultimately operates them. The organizations affected here look less like chosen targets and more like workplaces where individual employees found and used such a service to get access to tools they wanted.

That demand does not make the risk any smaller. A relay in this position sees every prompt, file, and secret an employee sends to the agent, and can alter or fabricate every response it returns. With the sandbox disabled and network access enabled, a malicious or compromised response could execute with the full privileges of the user's account. None of the evidence reviewed here shows the operator exploiting that position, but the architecture would support it if the operator's intentions or security changed.

The credentials this service issues do not stay confined to the AI agent, either. Because they are established as user-scope environment variables, any other tool on the same machine that reads those variables can pick them up, extending the exposure well beyond the coding assistant that first prompted an employee to install the service.

Protection

For the latest protection updates, please visit the Symantec Protection Bulletin.

If an IOC is malicious and the file is available to us, Symantec Endpoint products will detect and block that file.

Organizations concerned about unauthorized AI relay use should also watch endpoints running Codex or Claude Code for the following:

Changes to base_url or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in a CLI's configuration file.

sandbox_mode set to "danger-full-access" in ~/.codex/config.toml.

OPENAI_BASE_URL, CODEX_API_KEY, or ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN set as user-scope environment variables outside an approved deployment process.

A PowerShell iwr | iex or bash curl | bash invocation run shortly after, or in place of, npm install -g @openai/codex or @anthropic-ai/claude-code.

Traffic from AI CLI tools to destinations outside an allow-list of approved AI service endpoints.

Indicators of Compromise

File indicators

Network IOCs

aiok[.]me

sorryios[.]io

nuoda[.]vip

chat[.]nuoda[.]vip

rawchat[.]cn

sharedchat[.]cc

mirbuds[.]com

claudechn[.]com

vibe[.]skk[.]moe

hxxps://vibe[.]aiok[.]me/setup-codex.ps1

hxxps://vibe[.]aiok[.]me/setup-claudecode.ps1

Title: Your Attack Surface Is Growing Faster Than Your Team Can Respond
Context: As AI helps attackers accelerate reconnaissance and exploitation, organizations need to reduce the opportunities that make attacks possible in the first place
Full Text:
Security teams cannot keep responding faster forever. As AI helps attackers accelerate reconnaissance and exploitation, organizations need to reduce the opportunities that make attacks possible in the first place.

That requires a pivot toward prevention and a broader view of exposure. An unpatched application matters, but so do unnecessary administrative privileges, forgotten internet-facing services, or legitimate tools available to someone who never needs them. Individually, these weaknesses may attract little attention. Connected, they can create an attacker pathway to the systems and data the business depends on.

An exposure management strategy helps organizations understand these connections and act before an attacker does. For lean IT and security teams, it also offers a practical way to reduce workload: fewer opportunities for attackers can mean fewer alerts to investigate and respond to.

Why Is Exposure Management Crucial Now?

AI is putting pressure on security from multiple directions. Attackers can use it to accelerate their operations, while employees’ adoption of AI applications, assistants, and agents introduces additional access and interactions to secure.

Detection and response remain essential. However, making them carry most of the defensive burden leaves teams dependent on quickly identifying and interrupting every intrusion.

Meanwhile, many attack opportunities involve capabilities organizations already have. Bitdefender Labs’ analysis of 700,000 security incidents found that living-off-the-land techniques, which abuse legitimate tools, appeared in 84% of major attacks. Patching alone cannot address the unnecessary access that makes those techniques possible.

The challenge is operational, too. In the 2026 Bitdefender Cybersecurity Assessment, 38% of security professionals cited the overhead of maintaining hardening rules and exceptions as a barrier to shrinking their attack surface.

Organizations need prevention that adapts as their environment changes and fits the capacity of the people responsible for securing it.

What Is an Exposure Management Strategy?

Exposure management is the ongoing practice of identifying, prioritizing, and reducing weaknesses attackers could exploit across an organization’s attack surface.

It extends beyond vulnerability management. Software vulnerabilities are part of the picture, alongside misconfigurations, exposed services, identity risks, and unnecessary access to powerful tools.

An effective strategy connects three activities.

First, establish visibility into relevant exposures.

Second, prioritize them using context, including the assets an attacker could reach.

Third, reduce those exposures and reassess the environment.

This is continuous work because exposure changes whenever accounts gain privileges, services become publicly accessible, or business requirements evolve. Threat Exposure Management provides a framework for organizing that repeatable process. Technology supports the program; ownership and follow-through make it effective.

How Does GravityZone Turn Visibility Into Prevention?

Bitdefender GravityZone Exposure Management combines visibility, prioritization, and adaptive hardening to help teams remove attack opportunities.

Endpoint Risk Management identifies vulnerabilities and risky configurations. External Attack Surface Management adds an attacker’s outside view of internet-facing assets and services. User risk insights and Unified Identities help teams understand accounts, behaviors, and privileges that contribute to exposure.

There is also Attack Path Analysis, which connects findings into potential routes toward critical assets. That context can change the remediation order. A medium-severity vulnerability on a privileged user’s workstation may deserve attention ahead of a higher-severity finding on an isolated system.

It also helps teams identify shared points across multiple routes, where one change could interrupt several potential paths. The analysis models connections from available findings; teams still need to assess and implement the appropriate fixes.

However, teams can add automated action through GravityZone PHASR (Proactive Hardening and Attack Surface Reduction). It learns how each machine-user combination operates and restricts unnecessary access to tools and behaviors attackers like to abuse. Hardening can adapt as legitimate usage changes.

What Outcomes Should Organizations Expect?

The primary outcome of continuous exposure management is reduced opportunity for compromise. Closing an exposed service, addressing a dangerous configuration, or restricting unnecessary tool access can remove an opening or constrain an attacker’s next move.

Better prioritization helps teams direct limited resources to the most consequential work. For example, what if an administrator account connects to several potential attack paths? Removing unnecessary access may reduce exposure across multiple systems, giving the team a clearer reason to prioritize the change.

Dynamic hardening can also reduce the manual effort of policy maintenance. PHASR allows teams to review recommendations or use Autopilot to apply them. Changes are audited and reversible, and teams can grant access when legitimate work requires it. These safeguards help teams reduce risk while managing operational disruption.

A further outcome is clearer evidence of progress. Leaders can track changes in risk posture and new or resolved attack paths, connecting security work to the routes toward important assets that have been closed.

Reducing attack opportunities can ease pressure on teams of all sizes and especially lean teams.

How Can Lean Teams Put an Exposure Management Strategy Into Practice?

Start with business priorities: the systems, identities, and services whose compromise would cause the greatest harm. Establish visibility, identify high-risk exposures, and assign responsibility for reducing them. Reassess after changes to confirm progress and identify what needs attention next.

GravityZone Exposure Management supports and simplifies this approach within GravityZone or alongside third-party endpoint protection and EDR. Organizations can build on existing investments and extend their program with separately licensed capabilities, including automated patching, cloud security posture management, and GravityZone AI Visibility and Control.

The strategic goal is to make prevention, through continuous risk reduction, part of everyday security operations. This helps close attack opportunities before they become an incident.

Title: Beyond the Inbox: How Threat Actors Abuse Microsoft Teams External Chat for Initial Access
Context: This activity does not exploit any known Teams vulnerability; it abuses a legitimate, default-on collaboration capability
Full Text:
Summary

Arctic Wolf Labs has observed a recurring social engineering pattern in hundreds of cases where threat actors have used Microsoft Teams’ external chat creation feature for impersonation scams, or to deliver malicious files. A consistent pattern of attacker behavior has emerged across these incidents: the use of the same throwaway tenants, the same “IT Support (Internal)” display names, the same remote-access tools, and increasingly, the same payload domains.

In this report, we’ll explore our findings, examine how attackers weaponize the external access / federation feature in Teams to reach employees, reveal the infrastructure identified through Arctic Wolf’s telemetry, and discuss the defensive measures organizations can take to disrupt this attack chain.

Key Findings

Arctic Wolf analyzed more than 400 incidents involving abuse of the Microsoft Teams external chat functionality for social engineering activity and initial access.

Threat actors repeatedly used highly consistent IT-support impersonation tactics, including IT-themed display names, friendly-sounding first names, and “(Internal)” labels designed to undermine external-user warnings in Teams.

We observed a measured infrastructure shift, from disposable .onmicrosoft[.]com tenants toward attacker-controlled domains, with .top domains accounting for roughly half of observed paid-domain cases.

Arctic Wolf detects this activity at the ChatCreated stage, creating a window of opportunity to identify and disrupt attacks before a victim engages with the threat actor.

Context

Microsoft Teams ships with external access (federation) turned on by default, meaning any Teams user in another Microsoft 365 tenant can find, chat with, and call an organization’s employees, provided both tenants allow external access. This is the feature attackers most frequently abuse. This activity does not exploit any known Teams vulnerability; it abuses a legitimate, default-on collaboration capability.

How Threat Actors Establish Teams Identities

Threat actors commonly establish external Teams identities through newly created or acquired Microsoft 365 tenants. Between 30 to 40 percent of the cases we analyzed involved default *.onmicrosoft[.]com tenant domains. This default domain requires no verification and can be provisioned within minutes, giving attackers a functioning Teams identity with minimal setup.

Arctic Wolf observed that, even when using this default domain, attackers engineer the tenant’s sender name to read as IT infrastructure. We have supplied a list of the default *.onmicrosoft[.]com tenant names observed in use across multiple customers in the Appendix at the end of this report [1].

Arctic Wolf assesses that threat actors typically select a support-, IT-, admin-, network-, or helpdesk-themed word as the tenant name, optionally suffixed with the number 365, or the words online, portal, or a random number, to obtain a free tenant name. In a smaller number of cases, Arctic Wolf observed threat actors using legitimate company names in the sender’s tenant name to increase their credibility.

How the Attack Unfolds

In a significant number of cases, customers reported that the malicious Teams contact was preceded or accompanied by “mail bombing”, the flooding of a victim’s inbox with hundreds of newsletter or subscription confirmations within minutes. The email storm is intended to manufacture urgency and bury legitimate emails such as security alerts, with the Teams “IT support” message arriving moments later to offer to resolve the very same problem the attacker just created.

This reflects an abuse of trust: employees are generally trained to treat email with suspicion, but a message delivered from inside their Teams instance bypasses that learned caution.

Beyond email masquerading, Arctic Wolf identified a range of consistent naming techniques used by threat actors across customer alerts. The attacker’s Teams display name is central to the deception. Arctic Wolf observed the following impersonation display names most frequently, meaning the pattern occurs across multiple cases: [2]

Attackers append “(Internal)” to the display name so the recipient perceives the message as coming from an internal IT sender, even though Teams simultaneously labels the sender as External.

Reoccurring usage of friendly-sounding names, such as “IT Service Desk – Liam , IT Support (Scott McGhee)”, or “IT Service Desk (Matthew)”. Here, adding a first name makes the Teams message appear to come from a real member of their organization’s Service Desk.

In several cases, attackers used region-specific naming conventions tailored to the target’s locale: for example, “Supporte TI,” the French/Spanish variant of “IT Support.”

We observed roughly 100+ emoji markers ( 🛡 shield, 🛠️/🔧 tools, ✅ check) used in attacker display names: e.g., “IT Support 🛡| Corporate IT Service 🛠 (Internal).” This may be evidence of the use of AI such as ChatGPT and AI-related automation to create content and identities in support of this campaign.

Most recently, we observed the attacker/external Teams user adding the target organization’s domain or company name in their own display name to make the message appear more legitimate.

We also observed a recent shift toward paid top-level domains (TLDs) for tenant creation. Of the paid domains we identified in these types of scams over the past few months, approximately 50 percent of fake identities used the .top TLD, around 40 percent used a standard .com domain, and just over five percent used multi-level domains such as .com.pl, .com.vn, and .com.br.

This aligns with Sophos’s reporting on the STAC4749 / Chaos ransomware campaign, which found that attackers have moved away from onmicrosoft[.]com throwaway tenants and toward IT-themed .top domains for payload staging and command-and-control (C2), as the low cost of .top registrations allows for convincing “update/ security/support” hostnames. Arctic Wolf also observed repeated use of other common TLDs, including .com.br and .com.vn in activity reported during July and August.

In a subset of these custom domains, attackers deliberately configured DNS records to redirect web requests to the legitimate Microsoft or victim organization site to appear authentic.

Attack Chain for Teams Chat Creation

Attackers target organizations where external access is enabled. Chat creation itself is only the entry point. Arctic Wolf assesses that, once trust is established, the attacker’s immediate goal in most cases is to obtain hands-on-keyboard access through a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool.

We also frequently observed attackers using vishing (a direct voice call to the victim from within Teams) to secure RMM installation. In cases where attackers target multiple victims simultaneously, typically via automation, the initial contact begins with a Teams chat message instead of a call. The most commonly observed RMM tools used in relation to this scam were Quick Assist (QuickAssist.exe / msra.exe), AnyDesk, ScreenConnect (ConnectWise), TeamViewer, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, and LogMeIn.

Of these, Quick Assist is the most frequently used. This may be because it is built into Windows, signed by Microsoft, requires no installation, and only requires the victim to read back a six-digit code. When attackers seek persistence beyond the initial call, they pivot to a commercial RMM tool (AnyDesk, Atera, ScreenConnect, or a second platform such as Level, installed via msiexec), which provides an independent control channel that survives remediation of the original implant.

Arctic Wolf identified a consistent attack chain across successful exploitation cases and correlated it with chains previously documented by security vendors such as Microsoft and Zscaler:

Attackers commonly target multiple users within short windows of time (approximately five minutes) to increase the likelihood of success, most likely performed through automation. Once a victim engages, the attack chain reported by customers shows threat actors reaching payload execution in under 15 minutes. Arctic Wolf observed similar compression in its own data: several cases recorded concurrent credential-access detections (Kerberoasting, GoldenPAC-related) firing alongside the initial Teams alert, indicating the endpoint was already compromised by the time the chat alert was triaged.

In a subset of cases, attackers leveraged Microsoft’s notes. Attackers generally avoid pasting a URL directly into Teams, which would trigger Safe Links / ZAP scanning, and instead navigate to the payload themselves during the remote session. Consequently, endpoint and identity telemetry are essential monitoring surfaces alongside message scanning.

How Teams Chat Abuse Works

Threat actors using external Teams chat as an initial-access vector is not new. The practice was first documented by Microsoft in the Black Basta (Storm-1811) campaign in mid-2024, which used the now-familiar chain of email bombing → external Teams “help desk” → Quick Assist → QakBot/DarkGate/Cobalt Strike → ransomware.

The technique was later observed in the Cactus campaign and in 3AM and Chaos. Earlier this year, Zscaler reported on the GoGRPC campaign, in which Teams vishing and Quick Assist were used to deploy the GoGRPC backdoor.

Example Attack Observed by Arctic Wolf

Arctic Wolf recently identified a potentially novel infection chain leveraging external Microsoft Teams chat messages, in which the threat actor posed as an IT helpdesk employee to initiate the attack. In the case we observed, the attacker instructed the user to run a PowerShell command and launch the downloaded file. The initial payload retrieval was performed via PowerShell, and both actions executed under the victim’s account with a parent process of explorer.exe, reminiscent of ClickFix, though not disguised as a CAPTCHA.

Next, the PowerShell command downloads an MSI from Azure Blob Storage, which bundles a PowerShell script and a ZIP archive (archive6.zip). Approximately 30 seconds after the MSI is launched by the user, the bundled PowerShell script (cleaner.ps1) is dropped into the users’ AppData folder (AppData\Local\PowershellCleaner\scripts) and executed. The script cleaner.ps1 contains a large array of hexadecimal characters, preceded by an IEX instruction to execute the joined and decoded array; the resulting plain code is a loader that reads a block of AES-encrypted data, decrypts it using hard-coded key/IV and computes its hash. If the hash matches a hard-coded value, the resulting PowerShell is executed via ScriptBlock.

Ultimately, this is an obfuscated decryption and execution stub to build and run an additional PowerShell payload. The purpose of this final payload is to extract the pythonw interpreter and implant (ss.py), both from the bundled archive6.zip. After sleeping for five seconds, the implant is executed via pythonw.exe.

The implant then starts another MSI transaction that issues LDAP queries to Active Directory for all computer and user objects (filtering for both Category and Class) using the System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher PowerShell shortcut adsisearcher, formatting the attribute output as [sAMAccountName] – [description]. This information is then transmitted to C2 server endpoints that are randomly selected from a list of domains and URIs laid out in the implant’s code.

How Arctic Wolf Protects its Customers

From the newly created tenant, the attacker initiates a one-on-one chat, which avoids the visibility associated with group conversations. Microsoft records this first contact as a ChatCreated event, which Arctic Wolf assesses to be the primary detection opportunity for defenders. Our alerts most frequently fire exactly here, before the user has done anything.

Arctic Wolf combines multiple detection engines to identify suspicious external Teams chats. Drawing on observations from thousands of customer environments, Arctic Wolf maintains indicators of compromise (IOCs) associated with these campaigns, including impersonation-focused display names such as IT Helpdesk and Helpdesk Support as well as attacker-controlled tenant and domain patterns.

Arctic Wolf’s behavioral engine also monitors Microsoft tenants that initiate conversations with multiple Arctic Wolf customers. When activity from a tenant, account, or domain appears anomalous, particularly when combined with other signals such as email bombing or suspicious follow-on activity, Arctic Wolf flags it for investigation.

Arctic Wolf also tracks top-level domains that threat actors commonly use to create tenants, host payloads, or support command-and-control infrastructure.

Beyond monitoring the initial Teams-based social engineering lure, Arctic Wolf maintains detections for the remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools that attackers frequently push during these engagements. Arctic Wolf alerts on the execution of RMM tools that are not sanctioned or expected within a given environment, since the unauthorized installation of legitimate remote access software is a common technique used to establish persistence once a victim has been convinced to grant access.

Arctic Wolf also correlates behavior over time, flagging cases where an RMM tool installation is followed by reconnaissance commands, such as enumerating users, groups, or network configuration, and prioritizing these for investigation.

Conclusion

External Microsoft Teams chat has become an effective initial-access vector because it exploits trust rather than a software vulnerability.

Arctic Wolf has been able to monitor and protect our customers from these attacks with proactive defenses. Across the activity examined, attackers combined email bombing, convincing IT-support impersonation, newly created tenants and domains, and rapid social engineering to move victims from a seemingly routine chat to remote access, payload execution, and, in some cases, broader compromise.

The recurring patterns provide defenders with valuable opportunities to interrupt the attack chain. An unexpected chat from an external tenant, particularly one that follows an inbox flood or uses an IT-themed display name, should be treated as suspicious. Correlating ChatCreated events with endpoint, identity, email, domain, and remote-access telemetry can reveal the progression even when the initial interaction appears benign.

Defensive Countermeasures for Organizations

Most organizations have no legitimate need for open, any-tenant external chat. Per Microsoft’s guidance in Manage external meetings and chat with people and organizations using Microsoft identities, move from “allow all” to an allow-list of trusted organizations. Organizations can take the following proactive steps:

In Teams admin center → Users → External access, select “Allow only specific external domains” and add only the partner domains the organization actively collaborates with. Once an allow-list is configured, all other domains are blocked by default.

Block chat with unmanaged / Teams-consumer accounts, and disable the option that lets unmanaged users start conversations with your users.

Block federation with trial-only tenants, as attackers commonly prefer free or trial tenants for their minimal setup requirements:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -ExternalAccessWithTrialTenants "Blocked"

Enable “Allow my security team to manage blocked domains” so the security team can push blocks (e.g., the .top indicators listed in this report) through the Microsoft Defender Tenant Allow/Block List → Teams domains tab.

Harden the remote-access path: block or restrict Quick Assist to authorized IT roles (or remove it where unused), and block or uninstall unsanctioned RMM tools (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, ScreenConnect, Atera, Level, Splashtop) via Defender for Endpoint or application control. Alert on any RMM tool not deployed through the Arctic Wolf agent.

Because this attack vector relies on social engineering rather than technical exploitation, people and process controls are critical to closing the gap:

Out-of-band verification for all remote-access requests. Mandate a callback to the user’s registered number or an approval flow in a separate trusted app. An impersonator controlling the Teams channel can’t complete a verification that lives outside it.

Tell staff exactly how real IT reaches out (which channels, which domains, which named contacts), and that unsolicited external “IT support” is inherently suspicious (especially if it appears right after an inbox spam flood).

Train users to read the External tag and the real sender domain, and to never dismiss the Accept/Block, Safe Links, or first-contact warnings. Provide side-by-side examples of the organization’s real help desk communications versus an impersonator’s.

Conduct targeted training for personnel regarding the specific social engineering tactics used in this campaign. For those without the time to devote to creating security training resources from scratch, the Arctic Wolf Aurora® Managed Security Awareness and Training solution delivers easily digestible security lessons for employees, including regular phishing simulations and a “Report Phish” button.

Microsoft is also clearly taking this threat seriously too. They’ve now built end-user reporting for security directly into Teams, letting employees report a suspicious message or an external user with a couple of clicks.
