Title: Technical Advisory: PHP2Shell Pre-Auth RCE (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
Context: Bitdefender has not observed exploitation and Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring; to use the access the flaws give them, attackers must act on the server, and...
Full Text:
[CRITICAL] | CVSS v4.0 9.2 | No exploitation observed by Bitdefender | Patch immediately

TL;DR

PHP2Shell is a pair of critical pre-authentication remote code execution flaws (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CVSS v4.0 9.2) in the PHP worker process, and every unpatched PHP installation serving web requests is at risk, with Apache servers running mod_php at highest risk. Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 now; on 8.1 or older, which have no official fix, move to a supported branch. Bitdefender has not observed exploitation and Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring; to use the access the flaws give them, attackers must act on the server, and GravityZone detections cover those actions. For exact remediation steps including how to identify affected systems and assess for prior compromise, see What To Do below.

Advisory History

2026-10-22: Initial publication. Bitdefender telemetry shows no PHP2Shell exploitation attempts as of this date. Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring the situation.

Situation

The flaws were first discovered by lcfr_hax of Calif, which reported an unconditional remote code execution with a shared root cause to PHP on 2026-08-11. OpenAI independently reported the same root cause that day, Wiz Research reported on 2026-08-24, and OpenAI sent further attack vectors on 2026-09-18 (The PHP Foundation, “Today’s PHP security release and how we’re strengthening PHP security”, October 2026). Wiz Research demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against the WordPress, Drupal and Joomla container images and credits frontier AI models with substantially lowering the barrier to exploit development.

The coordinated disclosure held until two days before the planned release. On 2026-10-20 at about 15:00 UTC the CVE IDs began circulating online with a wrong release time and a CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). PHP published its pre-announcement early at 19:30 UTC and moved the release forward from 2026-10-22 to 2026-10-21 at 14:00 UTC. At about 20:00 UTC Calif mistakenly published a video showing its proof of concept working against a number of targets. PHP says no technical details leaked, but the video contributed to the faster development of various proofs of concept. On 2026-10-21 at 07:41 UTC Chainguard published container images containing the fix more than six hours before the release, breaking the embargo. PHP released the fixed versions at 14:00 UTC and published PHP, “Security advisory 2026-10-21-5”, October 2026 with them (The PHP Foundation, October 2026). PHP states that its security team identified no functional exploits at the time of release.

Datadog Security Labs, “PHP2Shell critical vulnerabilities”, October 2026 reports that AWS saw exploitation attempts from 2026-10-17, and describes broad untargeted scanning. Bitdefender has not independently confirmed this. Operational guidance is maintained by NCSC-NL, “PHP2Shell operational page”, October 2026 and in CERT-EU, “Security advisory 2026-018”, October 2026.

Several GitHub repositories claim to host proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. JFrog, “PHP2Shell: all you need to know”, October 2026 reports that some are pranks, one of which changes the victim’s wallpaper. Treat every unofficial PoC as untrusted code.

Bitdefender telemetry has observed no PHP2Shell exploitation attempts as of publication, and Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are monitoring the situation. This is a time-bound observation and not evidence that the threat is overstated. Any change will be recorded in Advisory History.

A Disclosure Is Not an Exploitation

Much of the early coverage of PHP2Shell blurs two different events, and the difference changes what you should do.

A vulnerability disclosure says a flaw exists, how severe it could be, and which versions fix it. The CVSS score of 9.2 describes what an attacker could do, not what any attacker has done. A disclosure carries no evidence that anyone is attacking anything.

A proof of concept is code that demonstrates the flaw. Proofs of concept range from working research tools to broken or malicious fakes, as the repositories above show. A working proof of concept lowers the cost of an attack but is not an attack.

Exploitation in the wild means someone has used the flaw against real systems that did not belong to them, and defenders have the evidence: requests, crashes, shells, files. Only this stage justifies statements such as “customers are being compromised.”

PHP2Shell sits between the second and third stages. It is disclosed and patched. Working proofs of concept exist in researchers’ hands, and Calif’s video showed one against a number of targets. PHP’s team saw no functional exploits at release. Datadog attributes exploitation attempts to AWS from 2026-10-17, which we have not confirmed, and Bitdefender telemetry shows none. Bitdefender Labs and the MDR team are watching for the next step.

Two conclusions follow, and they point the same direction. Do not treat the absence of confirmed attacks as a reason to wait, because the flaw needs no login and no application bug, and the proofs of concept and fixed code are public. And do not treat the severity score as proof of compromise: patch first, then check for compromise using the signals in What To Do, instead of assuming the worst.

How It Can Be Exploited

PHP runs behind the web server through a SAPI (Server API), the interface that hands each request to PHP. The two most common are mod_php, where PHP is loaded directly into the Apache web server’s own processes, and PHP-FPM, a separate pool of PHP worker processes that the web server forwards requests to. Both CVEs are memory corruption bugs, meaning the attacker causes PHP to read or write memory it should not, inside those worker processes.

On mod_php, exploitation happens during request initialization, before any application code runs. We assess that PHP2Shell is a runtime bug, not an application bug: on mod_php, CMS updates, plugin hygiene and application hardening do not change exposure. The attacker needs no login and no flaw in WordPress, Drupal or the custom code behind the site.

We assess with high confidence that exploitation attempts will follow. Calif’s video of a working proof of concept, Wiz’s demonstrations against common CMS container images, and Wiz’s report that frontier AI models lowered the cost of building exploits all shorten the path from disclosure to attack. The attack follows the established pattern for internet-facing remote code execution: scanning first, though version fingerprinting is unreliable here, then initial access through one of two paths. CVE-2026-109618 uses a single oversized request to corrupt memory while PHP is still setting the request up. CVE-2026-109619 reuses memory left behind by an earlier request on the same worker. No public source yet documents the automated phase, the hand-off to human operators, or post-exploitation activity for PHP2Shell specifically. The established pattern for comparable flaws is a first shell, a reverse shell back to attacker infrastructure, a webshell for persistent access, tool downloads, privilege escalation and persistence. These are the stages defenders should prepare for, not observed PHP2Shell behavior.

Exposure requires an unpatched PHP branch serving web requests. The demonstrated application-independent path is mod_php. CVE-2026-109619 additionally needs session.upload_progress.enabled left at its default of on, and attacker requests landing on the same worker, while its fatal-error-backtrace path applies to PHP 8.5 only. Several things limit how many attempts succeed: CVE-2026-109618 also requires defeating ASLR (address space layout randomization, which places code at unpredictable memory addresses), the same-worker requirement constrains CVE-2026-109619, and public PoCs are unreliable. Other factors widen the blast radius: no authentication, no application flaw needed on mod_php, and a default-on setting in the CVE-2026-109619 path. Wiz reports versions back to PHP 5.4 are affected, and branches 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 have no official fix. The version string is unreliable in both directions: distribution backports fix the bug without changing the version, so scanners flag patched hosts, while “latest available” on an end-of-life branch still means vulnerable. Exploitation attempts are reported by a named third party and are expected; successful exploitation at scale is not established.

Hunting guidance from other vendors, including Datadog, points defenders at crash evidence: memory exhaustion errors at initialization and Apache segmentation faults. A successful exploit can return HTTP 200 and leave the worker running. Crash logs measure attempts, not compromises.

If you have confirmed exposure, skip ahead to What To Do.

How It Works

CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption). An out-of-memory condition (PHP running out of its allowed memory) interrupts PHP while request data is only partly initialized, and the cleanup routine then treats the half-built data as valid. Datadog describes the trigger as an unauthenticated POST request with a single very long form field name, about 3.5 MB in the lab. When the attempt crashes or fails, PHP logs a memory exhaustion error reported as “Unknown on line 0”.

CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state). Request-owned state survives after its memory is freed, and a later request handled by the same worker reuses it. This is a use-after-free: the program keeps using a pointer to memory it has already released, which an attacker can refill with data they control. The path requires session.upload_progress.enabled, the setting that tracks file upload progress in the user’s session and is on by default. The fatal-error-backtrace path applies to PHP 8.5 only.

On Apache, a crashed worker appears in the error log as AH00052, the message Apache writes when a child process exits on a signal such as a segmentation fault. A successful exploit can avoid both this entry and the memory exhaustion error.

What To Do

The steps below expand on the immediate actions summarized in the TL;DR.

1. Identify Exposure

Read the PHP version and the Server API line from a phpinfo page served by the web server: a one-line file containing <?php phpinfo(); placed temporarily in the web root, which prints the running build’s configuration. Delete it immediately afterward, because it exposes that configuration to anyone who requests it. Do not rely on php -v, which reports the command-line binary and not necessarily the build the web server runs. On Apache, apachectl -M | grep -i php lists a loaded PHP module if mod_php is in use; systemctl list-units | grep php shows running php-fpm services. For distribution packages, search the package changelog for the CVE IDs, because a backported fix may not change the version number: on RHEL-family systems, rpm -q --changelog php-common | grep -E 'CVE-2026-10961[89]'; on Debian or Ubuntu, apt changelog php8.x-common | grep -E 'CVE-2026-10961[89]', substituting your branch for 8.x. For containers, check base image tags, especially WordPress, Drupal and Joomla images.

SAPI

Exploitability

mod_php

Application-independent RCE demonstrated

PHP-FPM

Susceptible; see the open PHP-FPM note in How it Works

php-cgi, FrankenPHP, LiteSpeed

In scope per PHP; no public exploitability analysis

2. Patch or Mitigate

Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35. Branches 7.4, 8.0, 8.1 and older have no official fix; moving to a supported branch is the only reliable answer, and unofficial backports are unvetted. PHP states: “there are no complete mitigations; updating is the only safe choice.” Where patching must wait:

Mitigation (all partial)

Addresses

session.upload_progress.enabled=0; on PHP 8.5 also fatal_error_backtraces=0

CVE-2026-109619

pm.max_requests=1 on PHP-FPM (each worker exits after one request, breaking the same-worker requirement; costs a process start per request)

CVE-2026-109619 on FPM

memory_limit=-1 combined with request-size limits at the web server or proxy and container memory limits; do not use the operating system’s per-process limits (RLIMIT_AS, RLIMIT_DATA) for this

CVE-2026-109618

WAF or reverse-proxy blocking

Both, partial

Restart all PHP workers after any configuration change; running workers keep the old settings.

3. Assess for Prior Compromise

A clean error log does not clear a host. Look for:

Very large requests in proxy or WAF logs, consistent with a multi-megabyte form field name. Request bodies are often not logged, so look at request size. This applies to CVE-2026-109618 only; no log signature has been published for CVE-2026-109619.

“Unknown on line 0” memory exhaustion errors and AH00052 entries (failed or crashed attempts).

Shell processes whose parent is a web worker (apache2, httpd, php-fpm, php-cgi).

New script files in upload, cache and tmp directories.

Start the lookback at 2026-10-17, the earliest attempts reported by Datadog. If you find a compromise, rotate the secrets the PHP process could read: application database credentials, API keys in environment variables or configuration files, and cloud credentials present on the host.

4. Monitor Ongoing

Watch this advisory, the PHP advisory and CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog for updates. Keep alerting on child processes of web workers, and keep software inventory current in GravityZone so hunting can be scoped to hosts running PHP.

Indicators of Compromise

Bitdefender telemetry shows no PHP2Shell exploitation attempts as of publication and we have no indicators of compromise to share.

GravityZone Coverage

The PHP2Shell exploit is memory corruption inside the PHP worker, so GravityZone detection focuses on what the attacker does with the access it gives: starting a shell, opening a reverse shell, planting a webshell, downloading tools, escalating privileges and persisting. These actions are where the attack becomes visible, and where the detections below fire.

Bitdefender MDR provides 24/7 threat monitoring and active response, and the MDR team is actively hunting for PHP2Shell together with Bitdefender Labs. MDR uses software inventory to scope hunts to systems running PHP, so keeping inventory current in GravityZone helps.

External Attack Surface Management (EASM) applies because the vulnerable PHP service is internet-facing: it identifies exposed assets from outside the perimeter without an agent, unlike Risk Management, which scans managed endpoints. EASM detects the PHP version on exposed assets, so it can show which of your internet-facing services run an affected version.

GravityZone Risk Management detects the PHP version installed on managed endpoints and compares it with data from the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) and the security advisories of specific Linux distributions (Ubuntu, CentOS and Red Hat). It flags vulnerable versions and the CVEs that apply to them.

The rules below come from Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR), Advanced Threat Control (ATC), and Proactive Hardening and Attack Surface Reduction (PHASR). Rules marked blocking stop the post-exploitation action, not the exploit.

Linux

Three detections work; however, PHP is deployed (Apache module, PHP-FPM or php-cgi):

First shell: Anomaly.Process.NewProcessStartedShell

Reverse shell: EDR.PhpReverseShell, ATC.BashReverseShell.X (blocking)

The rest of the Linux detections are tied to the web worker process and fire for Apache mod_php and php-cgi, not when the parent process is PHP-FPM:

First shell: EDR.WebServiceSpawnShell

Reverse shell: EDR.WebReverseShell (incident), the generic reverse-shell rule family

Hands-on activity: EDR.SuspiciousWebServerBehaviour and .2, EDR.Generic.Nexus.WebServer

Webshell: EDR.WebServiceWriteScript

Windows

On Windows, PHP typically runs as php-cgi.exe, and alerts such as SuspiciousExecution.PotentialPHPWebshell already monitor php-cgi and other web server configurations. ATC has heuristics that detect command shells started by php-cgi.exe when post-exploitation actions follow through those shells, such as enumeration, credential dumping or adding a new user to the machine. Because both flaws require heap manipulation (the attacker shaping how PHP lays out memory), Process Introspection also detects suspicious process creation from memory pages that do not belong to a loaded module. Process Introspection checks the state of a process during key operations such as creating a child process, which is where an exploited PHP worker would start a shell.

Hands-on recon: SuspiciousExecution.PotentialPHPWebshell (104852)

Webshell: SuspiciousServerRootFile (100942), WebShellCreation (102198)

Reverse shell: PossibleReverseShellSocketPipeChild and Parent (103945, 103946), PythonReverseShell (102194), the NetCat rules, Empire.Stager.WAR (105626)

Tool download: CertutilDownload, PotentialIngressToolTransferViaCURL

Persistence: NewScheduledTask, PowershellScheduledTaskCreated

PHASR (blocking): whoami, certutil, curl and PowerShell downloads, account creation, local admin group changes, schtasks

macOS (PHP under Apache httpd or php-fpm)

First shell: EDR.WebService.ShellSpawned

Reverse shell: EDR.Metasploit.PhpMeterpreter, EDR.Metasploit.ReversePhpSsl.N and Payload.ReversePhpSSL.Y, ATC.Metasploit.Payload.ReversePhpSSL.X (blocks on execution), the reverse-shell rule family, PHASR Bash reverse shell and Netcat (blocking)

Title: Unboxing Phishing Kits: Huntress Examines 3 Real Kits
Context: More advanced kits feature admin dashboards from where attackers can track their victims, modify phishing page content, and relay credentials in real-time
Full Text:
Teach a noob to phish and they'll be scamming for a lifetime. It has never been easier to steal credentials, thanks to a growing number of phishing kits that give aspiring attackers everything they need in one convenient interface.

Huntress Staff Threat Intelligence Analyst Andrea Hatcher and Staff Product Manager Rich Mozeleski stopped by our monthly Tradecraft Tuesday series in October to unpack some recently staged phishing kits and walk through what the resulting malicious activity looks like from the defenders' point of view.

Watch the full video below, and keep reading for clips and other highlights.

Example phishing kits

A phishing kit is a pre-packaged resource with code, templates, and instructions for how to launch a phishing campaign and use the stolen credentials for further malicious activity. Basic kits are often made up of simple HTML and script files that can spin up a single fake login page.

More advanced kits feature admin dashboards from where attackers can track their victims, modify phishing page content, and relay credentials in real-time.

Here are three of the many phishing kits that Huntress has analyzed in the last few months, all targeting Microsoft 365 tokens:

EvilTokens

Knight Office

Kali365

EvilTokens hops off the Railway

Just a few weeks before this broadcast, a collaboration between Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit and the FBI led to the arrest of one of the alleged operators of EvilTokens, a device-code phishing campaign that abused the Railway PaaS as a token-harvesting and token-replay engine.

For more on the EvilTokens takedown, watch Rich's conversation with Microsoft's Principal Corporate Counsel Carlton Gammons and Huntress' Chief Legal Officer Lauren Zajac on-demand.

As Rich put it, discovering the EvilTokens campaign in February "opened the dam" for our researchers diving into phishing kits. He noted the kit's professional aesthetic and 24/7 support as akin to a software-as-a-service (SaaS) operation.

Moving beyond passwords

Andrea walked through how the Kali365 control panel is an entire criminal ecosystem in a box, including AI features: "It's not just someone standing up a convincing login page, it's a whole ecosystem that helps an operator acquire infrastructure, collect authentication material, retain access, and even scale it up."

>

With these additional capabilities, phishing kits can help attackers get their hands on a lot more than usernames and passwords. We asked the audience what they thought attackers found most desirable these days, and most of those polled answered an authenticated session token or a persistent foothold.

Modern phishing kids can provide low-skilled attackers with a usable authenticated session with any of the following tactics:

Device-code phishing

Adversary-in-the-middle (AitM) phishing

Token theft and replay

Device-code phishing

Device-code phishing refers to when the user authenticates directly with the identity provider, but the attacker captures the resulting authorization. Device-code flows can reduce friction for attackers because they do not require the victim to surrender a password directly.

Rich shared that an estimated one in six incidents investigated by Huntress' ITDR team involved a rogue device being registered, and 36 percent of the audience members polled had seen device-code phishing in the wild. He points to Conditional Access Policies as a key prevention measure: "The vast majority of Microsoft environments do not need device code flow."

Adversary-in-the-middle attacks

AitM attacks reveal the limitations of MFA; the threat actor relays the authentication flow in real time, either with a fake login page or by intercepting an exchange within the legitimate app. The victim completes the MFA prompt while the attacker captures the resulting session information. This is why successfully completed MFA does not make the session trustworthy on its own.

Token theft and replay

As Andrea put it, "the session can be way more powerful than the password." After an attacker gets their hands on a sign-in token, a phishing kit can help them "replay" it into an active session, where they can access cloud resources and victim email accounts.

If you suspect token replay in your environment, your investigation should move beyond the original phishing page and examine how the token was used. Polled audience members voted sign-in address and new device registration as the top two signals to investigate first if token theft is suspected.

What defenders see, and what to do about it

Andrea emphasized the importance of detecting signals across the chain. One signal is weak; the sequence is strong. Correlate the progression of lure, authentication, token issuance or theft, device registration, mailbox activity.

Andrea drove the point home: "Join the telemetry across the identity provider, the endpoint, the browser context, the network, and the mailbox. We shouldn't just be looking at one signal in the network or one signal in the mailbox. We really need to have that holistic view."

Detection opportunities

Investigate successful sign-ins from unfamiliar cloud infrastructure.

Hunt for device-code authentication and automated token refresh.

Review new devices, authentication methods, and mailbox activity.

Response priorities

Containment must address identity artifacts, not just the original lure.

Revoke refresh tokens.

Remove unauthorized devices and Windows Hello credentials.

Restrict or block device-code authentication where possible.

Investigate mailbox access, forwarding rules, and outbound phishing.

Continue hunting after the original phishing domain disappears.

Continuous response loop

Detect correlated identity and endpoint activity.

Revoke or remove persistence mechanisms.

Investigate downstream mailbox and outbound-phishing activity.

Continue monitoring for replay or re-entry after containment.

Title: What’s New in GravityZone October 2026 (v 6.78)
Context: This section describes new functionality designed to elevate analysts' capabilities, offering enhanced tools for threat detection, investigation, and response
Full Text:
Bitdefender rolled out new functionality in Bitdefender GravityZone, a unified cybersecurity platform that provides prevention, protection, detection, and response capabilities for organizations of all sizes. These features, aligned with our multi-layered security strategy, are designed to reduce the workload for security analysts, administrators, and users.

What’s new for Security Analysts

As attackers increasingly blend into legitimate activity, security analysts must uncover signs of sophisticated attacks and make the invisible visible. This section describes new functionality designed to elevate analysts' capabilities, offering enhanced tools for threat detection, investigation, and response.

CLAIRE AI Assistant Enhancements (Early Access)

When an analyst opens an incident and needs to decide on containment, the assistant now starts from that page’s context instead of a blank prompt. CLAIRE, previously named GravityZone AI Assistant, is a conversational assistant built into the Control Center. It applies large language model (LLM) reasoning to Bitdefender Support Center documentation and to data from your GravityZone environment to answer questions, issue recommendations, and initiate selected response actions.

CLAIRE is available through a controlled Early Access Program (EAP). It now has its own entry in the GravityZone navigation menu, with a Chat page and an Advisor briefing page.

On the Incidents, Network, and Policies pages, a new chat opens with page-specific prompts, and coverage extends to the rest of the interface. As the conversation continues, CLAIRE suggests follow-up prompts. When asked to isolate the endpoints associated with an incident, CLAIRE builds the endpoint list for review, and isolation runs only after the analyst refines the list and clicks Isolate. Outside incident work, the Advisor briefing page lists proactive posture recommendations. Each recommendation’s details page explains why CLAIRE chose the issue, summarizes the top affected items, and suggests remediation actions.

The chat window also adds a Stop button that cancels a prompt before the response is generated. A message now appears when you reach your usage limit, and all chats now follow a 30-day retention period.

Attack Path in GravityZone Exposure Management

Attackers rarely reach a critical asset in one step. They chain a misconfiguration on one asset to an exposed account or vulnerability on the next. Attack Path is now available as part of the new GravityZone Exposure Management license. It correlates endpoint risk findings, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) data, and External Attack Surface Management (EASM) asset records to determine the most likely paths an attacker could take to compromise your assets.

Each attack path under Risk Management > Attack Path shows a graph and an asset list that mark potential entry points, exploitable vulnerabilities, and misconfigurations along the route. The graph can highlight the shortest path to the target asset, showing where a single remediation action breaks the largest portion of the chain. Risk factors such as Public exposure and Critical asset appear in both the graph and the asset table. When an asset also has a Risk Management entry, the asset details panel includes a button that opens the matching Risk Management > Resources or Risk Management > Accounts record.

Four new widgets on Monitoring > ASM Dashboard track attack paths across the environment:

New attack paths: lists newly created attack paths for Last 24 hours, Last 7 days, or Last 30 days.

Open attack paths over time: charts New and Resolved attack paths, with a trend line, for Last 7 days, Last 30 days, or Last 90 days.

Top 5 attack path destinations: lists the five assets that attack paths target most often.

Top 5 attack path entry points: lists the five assets that most often serve as attack path entry points.

For detailed information about Attack Path, see the dedicated TechZone article here.

AI Visibility and Control Enhancements

Unmanaged AI tools on endpoints are now a routine part of an organization’s attack surface, and assessing that exposure requires seeing it alongside other risk data. AI Visibility and Control (AIVC), is a discovery and risk layer that reports which AI software is installed and running on managed endpoints and assigns a risk score to each finding. This release extends AIVC data to the ASM Dashboard, the AI Services page, and Risk Management > Resources.

Monitoring > ASM Dashboard now includes a dedicated AI Visibility and Control smart view with an overview of AI usage and risk exposure across the organization. Its widgets show the overall AI risk posture, compare risk across AI categories, list the affected users and endpoints, break findings down by AI category, and list the discovered AI services. AIVC widgets can also be added to custom dashboard smart views.

On AI Visibility and Control > AI Services, each discovered AI service now shows its associated finding or finding count, in both the grid and the service details. From there, analysts can open the AI Findings page to investigate. AI-related findings also appear in Risk Management > Resources, so an endpoint’s AI exposure sits alongside its other risk data. From there, analysts can move between the affected resource, its findings, and the associated AI services.

For comprehensive insights into AIVC, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

EASM Enhancements

External Attack Surface Management builds an attacker-centric view of an organization’s internet-facing exposure. This release adds classification detail to similar domain findings, and maps discovered public IP addresses back to the managed servers that use them.

Similar domains flagged as potential brand impersonation attempts now identify the typo squatting technique used to construct them — misspellings, alternative top-level domains, and substitutions involving visually similar or keyboard-adjacent characters. EASM also highlights public IP addresses used for external communication by servers managed by Bitdefender Endpoint Security Tools (BEST), with the managed servers using each address viewable alongside it. Analysts can identify which addresses to add to the EASM scan list, giving Attack Path additional context on potential entry points into the organization’s network.

For comprehensive insights into EASM, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

EDR and XDR Enhancements

GravityZone Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) and Extended Detection and Response (XDR) give security analysts the tools to detect, investigate, and respond to threats across managed endpoints and connected sensors, with raw event telemetry that supports historical querying and incident investigation. This release changes how search is organized and shared and adds detail to incident and alert data.

Search and investigation

Separate menu entries: Historical search and Live search now appear as separate entries in the left-side menu of GravityZone Control Center.

Shared smart views: Smart views created on the Live search page can now be shared with other users in the company, with read-only or editable permissions. Company Administrators can edit, delete, rename, or make editable for any shared smart view, regardless of who created it or what permissions it has. Other users can delete, rename, or make editable only the views they created, and can edit only those they created or have edit permissions for. Shared smart views appear in a separate section of the Queries panel. Each one has a banner showing its access rights, creator, last update date and time, and the user who last modified it. Create, edit, and delete actions are logged on the User activity page, in the Live search area.

FQDN search: Historical search now supports searching and filtering raw events and alerts by endpoint-submitted fully qualified domain name (FQDN) values. The fqdn field is available in the query editor helper under the Other category, and other.fqdn can be added as a column in the results table and viewed in the event details panel.

Incidents and alerts

Entity type filter: A new Entity type filter under More filters on the Incidents page narrows incidents by the types of entities they contain. It supports multiple selections, and its options are populated from the entity types present in your incidents.

Self Protect attribution: In alert details for Endpoint incidents, alerts generated by the Tamper Protection module now show Self Protect in the Detected By field.

MITRE ATT&CK tactics: XDR and EDR incident and alert details now also support the Resource Development, Stealth, Defense Impairment, and Reconnaissance tactics. Activity previously classified as Defense Evasion may now be reported as Stealth or Defense Impairment, depending on the detection context.

Timestamps with seconds: Timestamps throughout Incidents and Historical search now include seconds as well as hours and minutes.

For analysts reconstructing an intrusion, the new tactics and second-level timestamps work together. A sequence in which an attacker disables a security service and then clears event logs within the same minute can now be ordered precisely, with each step mapped to Defense Impairment or Stealth.

For comprehensive insights into detection and response with GravityZone EDR and XDR, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

What’s new for Administrators

With administrators constantly juggling numerous tasks and responsibilities, they appreciate tools that make their daily work easier. This section describes new functionality designed to simplify managing features responsible for prevention, protection, and detection in a defense-in-depth security architecture.

Extended Email Security Enhancements

Bitdefender Extended Email Security (EES) offers flexible deployment models (Gateway, API-based, and Unified) to provide a comprehensive defense against sophisticated spear-phishing, brand impersonation, and supply chain fraud. This release adds outbound data loss prevention rules, distributor-level console access, and a confirmation step for identity provider sign-in.

DLP rules in Extended Email Security now also cover outbound email for the Gateway and Unified deployment models, which require Outbound Smarthost. Rules inspect the subject, headers, body, attachment types, URLs, and sensitive data patterns, including credit card numbers, International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs), and Social Security Numbers (SSNs). Matching outgoing messages are sent to Quarantine or deleted with Delete. You can apply enforcement globally or target specific customers, domains, or users.

Distributors and higher-level partners can now access the Extended Email Security consoles of the downstream partners they manage directly from the Extended Email Security section, across nested partner hierarchies, without Extended Email Security being provisioned for their own company. Console visibility follows the existing Your Bitdefender partner can assist you with security management settings, and the available actions are determined by Extended Email Security permissions within each accessible company. For detailed information, see the dedicated TechZone article here.

In addition, users who sign in with GravityZone credentials and open the Extended Email Security console now see a confirmation prompt. The prompt asks them to approve the automatic switch to the GravityZone identity provider (IdP) before proceeding.

For comprehensive insights into Extended Email Security, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

Security Data Lake Single Sign-On

Security teams that use Security Data Lake alongside GravityZone can now sign in to both with the same corporate credentials. Bitdefender GravityZone Security Data Lake combines SIEM operations with scalable data lake storage and advanced analytics, collecting and correlating data from multiple organizational sources for proactive threat hunting.

Security Data Lake now supports single sign-on (SSO) through GravityZone IdP Proxy, so users authenticate with their organization’s identity provider. GravityZone IdP Proxy supports SSO using SAML 2.0 and System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) to manage and verify digital identities across the GravityZone ecosystem.

With Security Data Lake added, sign-in to it is now handled by the organization’s existing identity infrastructure, the same as for the other GravityZone services connected through IdP Proxy.

Network Enhancements

The GravityZone Network inventory gives administrators a consolidated view of all managed endpoints, containers, and network assets across their environment. This release adds two network identifiers to the Network page and refines one filter option:

Public IP column and filter: Displays each endpoint’s public IP address, separately from the existing IP column and filter, which show the local IP address. The filter supports text matching with starts with or contains, so partial IP addresses also return results. Endpoints imported through integrations such as Active Directory, Microsoft Entra ID, VMware vCenter, or Amazon Web Services (AWS) do not display a public IP address.

MAC addresses column and filter: Displays each endpoint’s MAC address information with the same text-matching options. Devices with multiple network interfaces show all their MAC addresses in a single cell, and the filter matches any of them.

Golden Image role option: The Golden Image option in the Role filter now appears only when the feature is turned on for your company.

With public IP and MAC addresses searchable directly in the grid, administrators can locate an endpoint from a known address, match devices against data exported from external network or security tools, and narrow large endpoint inventories even when only part of an address is known.

Compliance Manager Enhancements

The Compliance Manager in GravityZone maps endpoint findings against regulatory and industry compliance standards, giving administrators a structured view of their organization’s compliance posture across managed assets.

This update adds two new compliance standards, now available across the Findings, Identity risks, and Compliance manager pages:

BNM RMIT 2025 (MY): Issued by Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM), the Risk Management in Technology (RMiT) policy document sets out requirements for financial institutions on technology risk management, covering technology governance, cybersecurity management, and operational resilience.

CSA Cyber Trust 2025 (SG): Issued by the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA), Cyber Trust is a risk-based certification mark for organizations with extensive cybersecurity measures and practices. The 2025 edition extends coverage to cloud, operational technology (OT), and AI security.

In addition, a new Notes column and filter on the Compliance manager page let administrators add and view notes for individual controls, such as justifications, context, or links to external documentation. Control notes can also be included when exporting compliance reports in PDF or XLSX format.

For comprehensive insights into Compliance Manager, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

Security Telemetry Enhancements

Organizations that correlate endpoint activity in their own Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) platform depend on the range and naming of the events they receive. Security Telemetry forwards raw operating system events from endpoints running BEST to a third-party SIEM. Administrators configure it in the Policy under General > Security Telemetry, where they select the event types to send. This release groups all events by category, adds descriptions for every category and event, and extends coverage with additional event types.

The Security Telemetry page now lists event types under named categories. Each category and event has a description, so administrators can see what an event captures before turning it on. The following categories and event types are now available:

Service: Added, Change status, Modify.

Scheduled task: Create, Delete, Modify.

Account management and authentication: Create local account, Delete local account, Logon failed, Settings changed.

Shell and script activity: Command Prompt command, PowerShell command, PowerShell script block logging, Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) buffer.

Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) job activity: Add file, Create, Delete.

Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) activity: Execution method, New activity, New binding.

Device and driver: Driver module load, Hardware mount, Hardware unmount.

BEST agent: Agent uninstall request.

Audit policy: Change Windows audit policy.

Process: Injection.

Existing event types now sit within the new categories under shorter names:

Process: Create and Terminate, previously Process creation and Process deletion.

File: Create, Delete, Modify, Move, and Read, previously File creation, File deletion, File modification, File move, and File read.

Registry: Create key, Delete key, Modify value, and Delete value, previously Registry key creation, Registry key deletion, Registry value modification, and Registry value deletion.

Account management and authentication: Logon, and Logout (renamed from Logoff).

Network: Connection and DNS query.

With command-line, PowerShell, and AMSI buffer events added next to service, scheduled task, and WMI activity, a SIEM can now correlate script-based execution with the persistence mechanisms that commonly follow it. Examples include a PowerShell command that registers a scheduled task, or a new WMI binding created shortly after an AMSI buffer event.

Firewall for macOS

Organizations that run mixed Windows and macOS fleets can now apply the same network traffic controls across both platforms. The GravityZone Firewall gives administrators granular control over network traffic, including which services and applications can communicate. The module, previously available on Windows servers and workstations, now also supports deployment and management on macOS endpoints.

Also, macOS support for the Firewall module carries through the Control Center areas that already handle Firewall on Windows: policy settings, installation packages, Threats Xplorer, Executive summary, Network, Reports, Dashboard, Health dashboard, Notifications, User activity, and the public API. The module requires BEST for Mac version 8.26.10.2000xx or later.

Policy rules now account for the platform they target:

Platform column: The Policies > Firewall > Rules table includes a new filterable Platform column that shows which operating system each rule applies to.

Existing rules: All rules previously defined in a policy are automatically set to Windows as their default platform.

Protocol support: The complete list of macOS-supported protocols is available on Bitdefender Support Center here.

The rollout of the Firewall module on macOS endpoints will take place in phases, so availability in individual environments may follow the console update.

Service API Keys

Automated integrations such as SIEM connectors, ticketing systems, and orchestration scripts often run on API keys tied to an individual user account, so the integration’s access depends on that user’s account and permissions. GravityZone now introduces dedicated service API keys and associated service accounts that manage automated integrations and API access independently of user API keys.

Service API keys are managed from the new Accounts > Service API keys page, with options to create, edit, clone, suspend, activate, and delete keys. You can configure each key with specific API module permissions, a target company and folder scope, and an expiration period of 1 to 365 days. Access to the page is controlled by the new Manage service API keys permission, available in the user account settings under Accounts.

Key lifecycle events are recorded in the User activity log, and administrators can receive email and Control Center notifications before keys expire. This keeps integration access auditable and scoped to the companies and API modules each integration needs.

More information about service API keys can be found on the Bitdefender Support Center here.

API Enhancements

Bitdefender Control Center APIs enable developers to automate business workflows. These APIs are exposed via the JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol. You can find usage examples and documentation in our Support Center, located here.

This update introduces new methods, push events, and response parameters to support incident assignment and tracking, service API key permissions, scan task visibility, network inventory, and macOS package configuration.

Incidents: The new assignIncident method assigns and reassigns Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) and Extended Detection and Response (XDR) incidents to eligible GravityZone users in bulk, and also removes assignees. All assignment changes are recorded in the Incident history panel and on the User activity page in GravityZone Control Center. Actions performed by Managed Detection and Response (MDR) analysts are attributed to an MDR Service account.

Event Push: Six new Event Push API events report EDR and XDR incident updates: incident-status-changed, incident-assignee-changed, incident-priority-changed, incident-note-created, incident-note-updated, and incident-note-deleted. They are turned on through the existing setPushEventSettings method. The Task Status push event payload now also includes the parentTaskId parameter for correlating parent tasks with their child subtasks.

Companies: The getCompanyDetails method now returns the status of companies undergoing migration between partners instead of a generic error.

Accounts: Accounts API methods now support the manageServiceAPIKeys permission, which corresponds to the Manage service API keys permission described in the Service API Keys section above. The createAccount, updateAccount, getAccountsList, and getAccountDetails methods now accept and return the updated role identifiers used with service API keys.

Network: The getTaskStatus response now includes the subTaskId (unique child task identifier) and scanType parameters in the subtasks object for scan tasks (Type 1). This identifies the scan type: Quick Scan, Full Scan, Custom Scan, Network Scan, Memory Scan, or YARA Scan. The getEndpointsList and getNetworkInventoryItems methods now also return the endpoint’s public IP address in the publicIp parameter.

Packages: The createPackage, updatePackage, and getPackageDetails methods now support configuring and installing the Firewall module on macOS endpoints.

For comprehensive insights into the GravityZone API, we invite you to watch our masterclasses here.

Title: The ballot box meets the bot.
Context: Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections.
Full Text:
State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security. Stolen credentials force ConnectWise to suspend cloud services. Fake calendar invites steal Microsoft logins. Temu settles Texas privacy allegations. Toronto police arrest seven in a cryptocurrency kidnapping case. The G7 sounds the alarm on quantum threats. Monday business briefing. Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

Today is Monday October 19th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security.

According to ProPublica, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security asked CISA to secretly acquire and hack a voting machine, then report its findings to the White House. Career employees resisted, concerned the results could be used to challenge election outcomes. The request was eventually dropped.

The revelation comes amid a dramatic retreat from CISA’s election security mission. Since President Trump returned to office, the agency has lost more than a thousand employees, roughly a third of its workforce, while cutting critical monitoring and support services.

State election officials say CISA was largely absent during preparations for November’s midterms. Meanwhile, the administration’s release of previously confidential election security information has damaged relationships built over years of cooperation.

CISA finally released an election security plan in late September, but state officials say it arrived too late to make much difference. Several now question whether they can trust the agency with sensitive information.

Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections. Election officials, candidates, and political organizations are attractive targets because of their access to sensitive voter and campaign information.

Attackers are using AI to produce convincing emails, text messages, and deepfake audio and video, eliminating traditional warning signs like poor grammar.

The agencies recommend phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, stronger email filtering, and independent verification of suspicious requests.

The alert describes an emerging threat rather than a specific ongoing attack.

ConnectWise suspends its Cloud Backup service following stolen credentials.

ConnectWise has suspended its Cloud Backup service and taken two other cloud services offline after attackers stole credentials associated with seven application identities, potentially exposing customer Microsoft 365 environments.

The stolen credentials allowed attackers to impersonate trusted ConnectWise applications without needing customer passwords.

Security firm Huntress identified suspicious sign-ins across roughly a thousand Microsoft tenants, including approximately 300 successful authentications. Researchers also observed a targeted campaign against 16 organizations in sensitive sectors, though those attempts failed.

ConnectWise says it has disabled the compromised credentials and found no evidence that encrypted backup archives were accessed.

However, backups and restoration services remain unavailable. Huntress warns that attackers may have established persistent access inside affected tenants before the credentials were revoked, making additional investigation essential.

Calendar invites steal credentials.

Cybercriminals are turning ordinary calendar invitations into credential-stealing traps. Researchers at Check Point identified more than 300,000 unique phishing emails targeting over 40,000 organizations, disguised as Microsoft Teams meetings and other workplace appointments.

The invitations contain links to counterfeit Microsoft login pages designed to capture usernames and passwords. Some include legitimate calendar attachments, making the invitations appear more convincing.

The campaign has accelerated dramatically, with Check Point recording more than 740,000 messages during the first two weeks of October alone.

Researchers emphasize that attackers aren’t exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft products. Instead, they’re exploiting employees’ familiarity with routine meeting requests.

Check Point recommends checking unexpected invitations carefully and using phishing-resistant authentication, such as passkeys or hardware security keys, to protect accounts against credential theft.

Temu settles with Texas over privacy allegations.

Chinese online retailer Temu has agreed to pay Texas three million dollars to settle allegations that it improperly collected user data potentially accessible to the Chinese government.

The agreement requires Temu to store personal data on U.S. servers and restrict transfers to China. It also mandates independent product safety testing and stronger consumer protections.

Violations of certain data security provisions could trigger annual penalties of eight million dollars.

Temu denies wrongdoing. Several other states have filed similar lawsuits, making Texas the first to reach a settlement.

Toronto police make arrests in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner.

Toronto police have arrested seven men in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner, including three active members of the Canadian Armed Forces.

Investigators say the victim was abducted at gunpoint in July, handcuffed, and assaulted as his captors attempted to access cryptocurrency holdings and business security systems. He was eventually released after being threatened not to contact police.

The investigation uncovered an extensive collection of weapons, including firearms with 3D-printed receivers, silencers, and more than 2,700 rounds of ammunition. Approximately 2,500 rounds were allegedly stolen from the Canadian military.

Police also seized substantial quantities of illicit drugs, GPS tracking devices, and other equipment.

The seven suspects face a combined 82 charges. The investigation remains ongoing.

The G7 urges post-quantum readiness.

The G7 is urging governments and businesses to accelerate their transition to post-quantum cryptography, warning that quantum computing could eventually undermine widely used encryption systems.

In a call to action led by France’s national cybersecurity agency, the group argues that quantum threats should be treated as a near-term concern, even though the timeline for developing cryptographically capable quantum computers remains uncertain.

The recommendations include identifying critical systems, inventorying cryptographic assets, and developing phased migration plans. Organizations are encouraged to incorporate quantum-safe technologies into routine equipment upgrades to reduce costs.

The G7 also calls for national strategies, additional research, public-private partnerships, and updated cybersecurity requirements.

France plans to begin rejecting security products without quantum-safe encryption during certification reviews starting in 2027.

Monday business briefing.

Investment in AI-driven cybersecurity continues to attract substantial funding, with eight companies announcing rounds totaling nearly $143 million.

San Francisco-based Harmonic Security leads the pack with a $50 million Series B, followed by Israeli startups Pluto Security, raising $42 million, and Rein Security, securing $25 million.

Other recipients include France’s Netsec and Fleuret AI, Tennessee-based Hilt, London’s CodeWall, and Utah’s Guardrail Technologies. The funding will support product development, hiring, and international expansion.

On the acquisition front, quantum computing company IonQ has agreed to purchase zero-trust security firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion.

CrowdStrike is reportedly negotiating a $500 million acquisition of Israeli data loss prevention startup Orion Security.

Meanwhile, government contractor SAIC has acquired cryptographic software provider Information Security Corporation, and Singapore-based V-Key has announced a majority investment in AI security firm CloudsineAI.

MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

MapQuest, the venerable mapping service that once helped drivers navigate the world with printed directions and a healthy supply of printer ink, has found a new way to stay relevant.

Its latest mobile app update introduces a surveillance layer that shows users the locations and directions of known license plate readers and outdoor security cameras.

The feature covers equipment from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions, Axon, Verkada, and several other surveillance vendors.

Flock alone reportedly operates at least 120,000 cameras across the United States, and independent projects have already been mapping their locations.

Now MapQuest is bringing that information directly into its navigation app, helping users identify surveillance infrastructure along their routes.

Apparently, the company that once helped you avoid getting lost can now help you see who’s watching you.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: Inbox flooded with sign-up messages? Email bombing explained
Context: First, an attacker gets hold of your email address
Full Text:
In September, reports emerged that a Virginia woman had been submerged by a flood of emails. Hundreds of automated messages poured in over a 24-hour period, including newsletters and promotions she’d never signed up to. But this was no ordinary spam campaign. The real reason behind the inbox blitz was to bury a legitimate email from the victim’s bank warning her about a fraudulent laptop purchase.

This is email bombing. And if it’s happened to you, it could be a warning sign that your identity or online accounts have been hijacked by fraudsters.

What is email bombing?

Sometimes called “form bombing,” “list bombing” or “subscription bombing,” email bombing attacks usually follow the same pattern. First, an attacker gets hold of your email address. They could do this from historic data breaches, marketing databases, online leaks, or even a prior phishing attack. Once they have it, they’ll use automated, bot-powered tools to sign up for hundreds or thousands of legitimate online services like newsletters, subscriptions, mailing lists, free trials, and competitions.

These will each generate a welcome email or similar. And because they are usually legitimate services, they’re often not blocked by spam filters. The result is an inbox overflowing with messages.

Why do they do it? Two reasons are behind most email bombing attempts:

The scammer is trying to distract the victim so that they don’t see a genuine email among all of the artificially generated ones. They may have hijacked one of your accounts and reset the password, triggering a notification to your inbox. Or they may have made a fraudulent purchase in your name, with the invoice subsequently emailed to you. The main point is to create a smokescreen which prevents you from tackling the more serious fraud.

The hacker may subsequently contact you pretending to be a tech support engineer. They’ll claim to be able to solve your email ‘problem’ and either request a fee to do so, or trick you into installing remote access software so they can take a look at your machine. That could enable them to steal sensitive information on your computer like passwords stored in the browser. Or even install additional malware.

In a corporate scenario, the bomber is most likely trying to distract the cybersecurity team from a more serious attack, such as a data breach or a business email compromise or invoice fraud attempt. Alternatively, they may be trying to disrupt operations as leverage for extortion – ransomware affiliates have used email bombing as a precursor to a fake IT help desk contact in order to get remote access. Or it could even be a disgruntled employee or former worker.

I’ve been email bombed: what next?

If you’ve logged on to find your inbox overwhelmed, don’t panic. Rather than try to unsubscribe to all of the random services you’ve been signed up to, focus your energy on finding the threat that your attacker wanted to hide. Search for security alerts, new device sign-ins, email/phone number changes, password changes/resets, or purchases. Look through your spam folder as well as your inbox, in case the message has ended up there.

If you don’t immediately see anything out of the blue, check your most sensitive accounts individually. These could include

Bank/PayPal/credit card/crypto

Apple/Google/Microsoft

Social media accounts

Look for any suspicious activity: new devices or payment methods added, passwords that may have been changed, and/or recovery details altered. It’s also worth checking your email forwarding rules and sent/deleted items folders for anything unusual.

If you notice something unusual, try to lock the hacker out by changing the password to a unique, strong credential, and enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for extra login security. Ensure the correct recovery email address/phone number is listed (or they may be able to reset the account again). Contact the company itself if you’re concerned about fraud.

Remember to preserve anything related to a possible account takeover or fraud attempt. Only purge when you’re confident it’s over. You can do this more quickly by trying to identify patterns in the messages (e.g., senders, date ranges, domains, etc.). Then you can bulk select and delete in batches.

It goes without saying that you should put the phone down immediately if anyone calls you claiming to be a tech expert who can sort out your email problem.

How to prevent email bombing

Of course, prevention is usually better than cure. And while it’s not always possible to stop your email ending up in the wrong hands, you can limit the damage by ensuring that it’s not exposed on public-facing web pages like social media profiles. Also follow security best practices to stay safe from phishing attacks.

Next, keep your most sensitive accounts as secure as possible. This includes your primary email address, which will be used to receive password reset messages from other online accounts. Use a password manager to ensure they all have strong, unique credentials. And 2FA for an extra layer of security (e.g., via an authenticator app or passkey).

It may also be worth using a secondary email address for less important correspondence like shopping, travel and other leisure activities. This way, if this account is hit by an email bomb, at least your most important messages (bank, government, healthcare etc) are safe.

There’s no silver bullet to prevent email bombing. But account security best practices will help to reduce the chances of an explosion of messages in your inbox.

Frequently asked questions (FAQs)

Why is my inbox full of hundreds of sign-up emails?

You may be the victim of an email bomb (aka form bomb/list bomb/subscription bomb). A fraudster has used automated tools to sign your email address up to new services for one of two reasons. Either they’re hoping to bury a legitimate security or anti-fraud message, or they’re going to call you pretending to be a tech support engineer that can help.

Has my email account been hacked if it’s full of sign-up emails?

Probably not. Fraudsters may have scraped it off the public web, harvested it from a historic data breach, or even bought it from a marketing database. However, the security/fraud ‘event’ they’re trying to hide with the email bomb tactic may have involved account takeover.

My inbox is full of new messages; what should I do?

First, search for the notification they’re trying to hide in the spam and preserve it. Search for security alerts, new device sign-ins, email/phone number changes, password changes/resets, or purchases. Look through your spam folder as well as your inbox. If you don’t find the message, check your sensitive accounts (bank, social media, tech etc) for unusual activity. Change passwords to a unique, strong credential, and add enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for extra log-in security.

I’ve been email bombed. Should I unsubscribe to all of the new emails?

No, it’s important to find the security notification or fraud warning the attacker is trying to hide, and preserve it. Only purge once you’re confident the issue has been resolved. Consider speeding up the process by deleting in batches (search for common senders, date ranges, domains etc.).

What if someone contacts me to fix the problem?

They’re a fraudster who wants to charge you a fee or trick you into installing remote access software on your machine, which could lead to malware or data theft. Put the phone down on them.

Title: Technical Advisory: AhsayCBS Exploitation Chain (CVE-2026-105133, CVE-2026-105134)
Context: Technical Advisory: AhsayCBS Exploitation Chain (CVE-2026-105133, CVE-2026-105134) #SMB Security #Enterprise Security #Ransomware #Threat Research By Martin Zugec / Oct 15, 2026...
Full Text:
[CRITICAL] | CVSS 10.0 (CVE-2026-105134, per VulDB) | Active exploitation confirmed, listed in CISA KEV | Patch immediately

TL;DR

Attackers are chaining two vulnerabilities in AhsayCBS, the server-side backup management platform of the Ahsay Cloud Backup Suite: CVE-2026-105133, an authentication flaw, and CVE-2026-105134, an OS command injection flaw rated CVSS 10.0 by VulDB. Every AhsayCBS v7 to v10 server that an attacker can reach, and that runs a build below v10.3.4.45 (v10) or v9.15.2.70 (v7, v8, v9), is exposed. That includes servers on the earlier patches v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59, which the Ahsay announcement, October 2026 says did not fully fix the flaws. If you have already patched, you are not necessarily safe: verify the installed build, apply the new hotfix, reboot, and check for prior compromise. Patching closes the entry point but does not remove webshells or other access an attacker has already planted, and that access can sit unused for weeks before a ransomware or data theft attack. Bitdefender MDR has investigated multiple incidents at our customers through this chain since around 7 October 2026. For exact remediation steps, including how to identify affected systems and assess for prior compromise, see What To Do below.

Advisory History

15 October 2026: Initial publication, based on three Bitdefender MDR incident investigations. Vendor hotfixes are available, and both CVEs are listed in CISA KEV.

Situation

AhsayCBS is the server side of Ahsay’s backup product. It receives, stores and manages backups for the clients connected to it. Attackers are exploiting two flaws in its web-facing components in the wild. The timeline:

4 October 2026, 07:16 UTC: Both CVEs are published in the US National Vulnerability Database (NVD). Both entries state that a public exploit exists.

Around 7-8 October 2026: Bitdefender MDR’s first two incidents begin. They coincide with the first public reporting of exploitation and the first Ahsay advisories.

12 October 2026: Ahsay releases hotfixes (v10.3.4.45 for v10, v9.15.2.70 for v7, v8 and v9). The same advisory states that the earlier patches, v10.3.4.0 and v9.15.2.59, did not fully address the vulnerabilities.

14 October 2026: CISA adds both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. KEV is the US government’s list of flaws with confirmed in-the-wild exploitation, and federal agencies must fix listed flaws by a set deadline. MDR identifies a third incident the same day.

17 October 2026: CISA’s federal remediation deadline.

Bitdefender MDR investigations and the KEV listing both confirm exploitation. Some indicators in our incidents overlap with publicly reported activity. We do not attribute this activity to any named actor.

The NVD entries still list 10.3.4 as unaffected. The vendor’s later advisory supersedes that statement, and this advisory follows the vendor.

How it’s Exploited

Backup servers are a valuable foothold. They hold credentials for the systems they protect and the storage they write to, and they control the copies an organization relies on to recover. A ransomware operator wants to steal or destroy exactly that data before encrypting anything else. AhsayCBS exposes a management web service so administrators and clients can reach it, so on many deployments the server is reachable from the internet by design.

All three incidents Bitdefender MDR investigated began the same way, through a combination of the two CVEs. One flaw breaks authentication. Improper authentication means the server can be tricked into treating an unverified request as legitimate. The other is OS command injection, where text supplied by the attacker is executed as an operating system command on the server. Both NVD entries name the same argument, random, and neither flaw needs an account or any user action. MDR saw the two used together. NVD, however, scores the command injection as needing no privileges on its own, so an attacker may not need the full chain to run commands. A public exploit exists. CISA’s Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC) is the model CISA uses to prioritize fixes, and it rates exploitation of both flaws as active and automatable.

Once inside, the attackers moved to confirm and test their access. In the first incident, they validated access through JSP webshells, which are small scripts planted on a web server that let an attacker run commands through ordinary web requests. They also staged PowerShell payloads, tried to stage payloads as command files (.cmd) in the shared C:\Users\Public folder, and tried to establish persistence, meaning a way back in that survives reboots and password changes. MDR analysts detected and blocked portions of this activity early. In the second incident, the attacker deployed JSP files (Java Server Pages, which act as webshells on this Java-based server) and again tried to stage command files in C:\Users\Public. The attacker then ran reconnaissance aimed at finding stored credentials, elevated a user account to SYSTEM (the highest privilege level on Windows), and used obfuscated PowerShell commands to install and configure OpenSSH, the standard remote-login service. A working SSH service would give an attacker a way back in that does not depend on the vulnerable web service, which is why patching alone does not end the incident. The attacker tried to establish persistence before being detected. In the third, MDR blocked and remediated the activity early in initial access. MDR credits three things: it identified known clusters of attacker behavior, the customer responded promptly, and configurations were reviewed quickly.

After that shared start, the incidents diverged. File names differed, the attackers abused different system tools and binaries, and the apparent objectives did not match. The Bitdefender MDR assessment is that the exploit chain was the constant, while file names, tools, and binaries changed from one incident to the next. Some indicators did overlap between the first two incidents, and the campaign appears to share some infrastructure: the C2 address 38.60.252[.]110 was the starting point of the two first incidents. Even so, a hash or file name from one incident may not reliably find the next one. The reliable signal is how the server behaves after the exploit fires. Combined with the differences between incidents, the shared infrastructure suggests a fluid situation in which several different actors may be using the same exploits. That is an assessment, not a finding, and it may change as more incidents surface.

Exposure conditions. Your server is exposed if two things are true. It runs AhsayCBS v7, v8, v9 or v10 below v9.15.2.70 (v7 to v9) or v10.3.4.45 (v10), and the attacker can reach its management web service. Servers on the earlier patches are not safe. An administrator who patched to v10.3.4.0 or v9.15.2.59 did the right thing at the time, but the vendor now says that fix was incomplete. The question to ask is not “did we patch?” The question is whether the server runs v10.3.4.45 or v9.15.2.70 or later.

Amplifying factors. VulDB, the CVE Numbering Authority, scores the command injection 10.0 under CVSS 3.1, the industry’s standard severity scale. A public exploit exists, and exploitation is rated automatable. The incomplete first patch leaves administrators believing they are covered. MDR’s assessment is that several actors may be using the chain. The credential reconnaissance in the second incident fits what backup servers hold.

Limiting factors. Exploitation requires network access to the management web service, so servers reachable only from internal networks carry less realistic exposure. MDR blocked one incident early in initial access and blocked part of the activity in another. MDR saw no encryption, data exfiltration or ransomware deployment. Ransomware remains a plausible risk because of the target type, but MDR did not observe it.

Confidence. This is observed in the wild, confirmed by first-party MDR investigations and corroborated by the KEV listing. We are not hedging on severity. This is internet-exposed, unauthenticated remote code execution with a public exploit, and in MDR’s assessment several different actors may be using it. That makes it a playbook case: continued opportunistic exploitation of unpatched and earlier-patched servers is near-certain. We are deliberately restrained on everything else. Three incidents cannot establish who is behind this, how many groups are involved, or what they ultimately want.

If you have confirmed exposure, skip ahead to What To Do.

How it Works

Public disclosure of the mechanism is limited. Everything below comes from the NVD entries and Bitdefender MDR observations, and nothing here speculates on root cause. Each flaw carries a CWE classification. CWE (Common Weakness Enumeration) is the standard catalog of software weakness types.

CVE-2026-105133 (improper authentication, CWE-287). The flaw is in the checkSysPwd function of the API component, in ApiStructsAction.java. Manipulating the random argument results in improper authentication. It can be exploited remotely, with no privileges and no user interaction.

CVE-2026-105134 (OS command injection, CWE-77 and CWE-78). The flaw is in the Replication Receiver component, the offsite store that synchronizes backup data from one or more AhsayCBS servers (Ahsay, “CBS v9 Replication Guide”, August 2025). The affected endpoint is /rps/api/json/UpdateReceivers.do. Manipulating the same random argument leads to OS command injection, again remotely and with no privileges or user interaction.

Why is this possible? NVD classifies the two as different weaknesses: improper authentication in CVE-2026-105133 and OS command injection in CVE-2026-105134, both reached by manipulating the random argument. Ahsay has not published why the first patches fell short, and we will not guess.

Scores. VulDB assigned all scores below as the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), the organization that issued these CVE IDs. NVD reports them but has not published scores of its own.
